speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Alex Yam, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our Housing and Development (HDB) public flats have influenced our way of life and Singapore society since Independence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As we continue to develop and evolve as a future-ready city, our housing policy will similarly evolve.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One pertinent question is how housing in our future-ready city will potentially integrate and how accessible they will be to ordinary Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our current Central Business District (CBD) has several pockets of public housing.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The reasons for this very small concentration are obvious.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The prices were high and available developmental space was limited.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Trying to plant in pockets of public amenities and housing resulted in the creation of very small enclaves.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, what about our new CBDs in Jurong and the greater Southern Waterfront?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I sense an opportunity to have better urban integration.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One such example of integration would be Vienna's post-war experience.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Much of the historic city lay in ruins after World War II and Austrians had the unenviable task of rebuilding their capital.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the 1945 Vienna Reconstruction Conference, a 14-point plan was introduced which, at its heart, stood this very particular vision that: "The human-being should in future stand at the centre of all considerations and plans, and not in the income and profit of the few".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Between 1947 and 1958, Vienna completed rehousing of residents with much of the social housing integrated into a reconstructed city.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This was followed by an urban housing rehabilitation programme between the 1970s and 1980s.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As the city expanded, housing areas saw revitalisation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Rather than standing apart, they became an unmistakable part of the cityscape.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Vienna had the opportunity to develop this successful social housing model because the city itself was in need of major reconstruction after the war.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While Singapore is not emerging from a post-war crisis, we similarly have an opportunity to do so, as we journey towards a future-ready city.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Viennese were bold in their approach in the revitalisation efforts from the 1980s.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A mix of social housing, council estate, apartments, condominiums and commercial properties were offered side by side in revitalised estates to achieve a better social mix, regardless of class, income and background.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At the end of the Cold War, there were further challenges to development with an influx with the fall of the Iron Curtain and, therefore, they were able to explore radical ideas for metropolitan housing.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These include the concept of developers' competitions, which were open to all firms, public and private, leading to unique estates, such as the car-free Autofreie Mustersiedlung − I would first apologise to anyone who speaks Austrian by my mangling of the names − the family-centric Frauen-Werk-Stadt, which was designed by women architects, built by women engineers; and a very ecological term Thermensiedlung, which is heated by natural hot springs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I believe Dr Lim Wee Kiak has a question on the Sembawang hot spring, so perhaps this is something to consider.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even today, despite political changes in Austria and a more centre-right leaning public policy, at least half of all new subsidised apartments in Vienna would be built in the inner-city areas.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A strong Social Architecture and Citizen Participation system dominates Vienna and entrenches the belief that urban developments and housing cannot be left completely to the free market.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is important at this point to note certain important caveats.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: First of all, Singapore does not have the luxury of land as the Viennese have.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Thirdly, unlike Singapore's core home ownership policy, 80% of Viennese currently live in rental apartments, due partially to the 1917 Tenancy Act which sets a cap on the maximum rent collectable.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In Singapore, we have a successful housing policy and our HDB housing is often cited along Vienna as two examples of how a city or a city-state can provide comfortable and affordable housing for its citizens.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Vienna sees value in Singapore's lessons in intensification.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can also learn from Vienna in seamlessly integrating social housing into the fabric of their city and also promoting civic participation in the development process.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In terms of future housing in Singapore, many people aspire to projects, such as the Pinnacle@Duxton, but there is certainly a worry though.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Though the price was also inflated due to the scarcity of supply, housing in Singapore has largely been influenced by location.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But overall, my focus has been to look at how we can build communities in our future-ready city, not just infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To be able to look at achieving a new integrated city that focuses on community, rather than just the economy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our future-ready city should not be cold, hard monuments to the pursuit of economic growth but also serve as focal points for the aspirations of citizens.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If we can successfully integrate a balanced neighbourhood that has a good social mix, avoids gentrification, and one that looks after the interests of many, will be one city, one nation that we can be proud of.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We should be sensitive to three things: honouring the past; acknowledging current challenges; and moving everyone forward.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In honouring the past, we need to protect our heritage and preserve our history.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Progress is often relentless and unkind, but not having a past, not recognising where we have come from means the future can only be bleak and soul-less.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, I urge the Ministry to do more to promote our built heritage and also preserve the intangible memories that come with them.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In acknowledging our current challenges, we need to be cogent to what hurdles some may face within our midst.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Divorcees who feel they are dealt a double whammy when housing becomes a problem, singles who feel they are hard done by, vulnerable families who feel that they cannot progress in a housing market that is geared against them, younger Singaporeans who want to live close to their parents but are priced out of the resale market.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This will have a positive impact on young Singaporeans wishing to settle down in a flat of their own close to their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The end losers would be buyers unable to fulfil their genuine needs and the Government which may be blamed as helpless and being unable to rein in unfair marketing practices.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Would we have a future-ready solution to deal with a future problem?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Lastly, how do we ensure that everyone moves forward together as we journey towards a future-ready Singapore?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As our population ages, we will need to provide for our seniors to age in place and to age gracefully with family and in the community.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Are we planning ahead of the curve and ensuring that a youthful and vibrant city does not abandon nor alienate our older residents?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The lower-income, the vulnerable should also not be made to feel unwelcome in the future-ready city.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As they stare down current challenges, they must not be met by a cold wall when the future arrives.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While many of our new attractions are free and accessible and our city has redeveloped and is reshaped, one cannot but feel pressured by prices and costs of everything else in that same space and also feeling out of place.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I remember one resident, an older resident, sharing with me that it is nice to visit these places, but just try getting an affordable drink or meal at Gardens by the Bay or Sentosa or even in the city itself.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Ministry of National Development (MND), HDB and the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) will have their work cut out for them, looking not just at how to shape up our future city but to also make it viable and open to all.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I would urge that greater citizen participation in the process will only prove helpful.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I, therefore, look forward to our future-ready city, but I also hope that it is one that is future-ready for all of us and not just for some of us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: There are several types of CPF Housing Grants, each catering to different types of buyers, such as whether they are applying for the first time and the citizenship of the spouse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The grant increase is aimed at making HDB resale flats even more affordable for the target group.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But by driving up demand, will they have the effect of also pushing up prices?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The prices of HDB resale flats are correlated with those of private property residential units.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Although HDB resale prices have moderated, this did not occur before the private property cooling measures were introduced.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: When sellers of HDB flats look for replacement housing, they add to the demand for residential property.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Any increase in demand for HDB resale flats will feed into the private property market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In this way, the impact on the overall property market is unavoidable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The market for HDB resale flats continues to be very active and is hardly in a weak state.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I understand the need to prevent property bubbles so that homes remain affordable.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But with the implementation of the Total Debt Servicing Ratio (TDSR), are the rest of the property cooling measures still relevant?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, the Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD) for Singaporeans.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many Singaporeans who have the income to spare would like to invest in private property.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, due to ABSD, they have turned to the overseas markets.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some ended up buying in ghost towns or buying from plans that never get built and they would never be able to recover their hard-earned money.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Besides that, Singapore is losing out on these funds.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Was this considered when weighing the retention of ABSD?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government consider removing ABSD at least for Singaporeans?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Government has already implemented TDSR as a policy measure to cool the property market.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some Singaporeans want to invest in properties, but because of ABSD, they have turned to overseas markets instead.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This has not only caused capital outflow from Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What is worse is that some Singaporeans may end up losing their hard-earned money.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Government consider removing ABSD at least for Singaporeans?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, please take your four cuts together.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That is an increase of three months every year or six hours per day.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singaporeans' life expectancy is increasing by 3.5 years every decade.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the national level, current policies must be redefined and even revamped to prepare for these 100 years of life.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If our workers are living up to 100 years old, it means that we have to work longer or save more.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, the issue of assets becomes a very important consideration for many of our older citizens.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I have come across residents who have downgraded their housing to a smaller unit even though their desire is to remain at the flat that they had lived for a long time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Housing is one of the most basic needs for everyone.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: In society, there is a plethora of family circumstances and needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: While we cannot fulfil the needs of all, advancing some aspects of the policies may help certain families.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: I will focus on two groups here − single parents and young couples with a foreign spouse.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Both groups are typically single income or no income for some, especially the single parents.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Being a sole breadwinner, some have to undertake two jobs to make ends meet.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: I agree that the Minister had earlier replied in a Parliamentary Question (PQ) that this can be managed through an appeal process and many have been assisted.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Although help has been rendered, often, single parents are under enormous anxiety with the looming uncertainty whether a shelter is immediately available after divorce proceedings.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: And to prevent those from gaming the system, a longer Minimum Occupation Period can be imposed.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: For those already living in rental flats, they have a different challenge.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: With the progressive wage structure, it is likely that they would be earning an income of at least $800 to $1,000 per household.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: With wage increase over time, some of them found that the increase in their wages has been used to pay off the increase of the quantum in the larger rental rates that they are paying.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: This deprives them of any savings towards owning their next flat.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: And for the single parents, I would think the issue here is that they have a short timeframe from the disposal of their flat to moving out of its premises.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: What more can the Ministry do to support transition home planning for these families?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Since the LBS was introduced, we have encouraged the elderly who need extra cash to unlock the value of their asset.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: There are takers for the scheme but seemingly not very high.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Some of their concerns are: one, lack of understanding of the scheme; two, unsupportive spouse or family members preventing them to proceed; three, no Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA) in place.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: For some elderly who live in 5-room flats or larger, this has resulted in conflicts because they do not have spare cash and they generally have fewer subsidies because of their flat type and some do not belong to the Pioneer Generation.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: This will help alleviate concerns in different situations and reduce the burden of costly legal processes subsequently.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: To assist married couples to obtain their first flat sooner, several measures have been introduced.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: But what about their elderly parents who wish to move closer to their children to provide extended family support?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: And our last group would be the private landed elderly home owners who wish to downsize to an HDB flat over time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The debarment period rule after the sale of their private property does not help to ease their transition.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Even for the resale HDB flat, they need to dispose of the private property within six months.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: This will be challenging during economic downturns or when the property market is weak.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Many would not have cash and they cannot borrow from a private bank loan.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: What can be done to assist them to downsize?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many families, children especially, are looking forward to a stable life in their new homes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But while the scheme caters to second-timer families with young children, "married, divorced or widowed" applicants, what about the single parents?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, children born under any sort of circumstances are innocent and should not be denied an equal footing in society simply because of their birth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They already have a more challenging start because they only have one parent.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Moreover, bringing up a child single-handedly requires a lot of strength and courage, and single parents should be respected for that.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, in relation to single parents, I hope more can be done to help them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Examples could include offering more flexibility to access housing, waiving the levies and providing child benefits as long as the parents are looking or holding on to their jobs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Their children, at the very least, deserve the same benefits as all other children in Singapore are entitled to.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I tell the story of HDB's beginnings to the students that I teach with real pride.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I remind them that we were once labelled by the British as having "one of the world's worst slums" because so many of us here were living in squatter conditions.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I tell them also about a man called Lim Kim San who was so affected by the struggles of the poor that he volunteered to chair the HDB and power his way through bureaucratic red tape and rigid regulations to ensure that low-income Singaporeans could gain quick access to low-cost housing as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The foundations of the HDB story were one marked by an urgent compassion and an ambition for social impact, and that is why it is regarded as one of the most successful social housing schemes in the world.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And I do see the continuation of Lim Kim San's extraordinary legacy whenever I hear stories of compassionate officers in the Public Service working quietly and ambitiously to help every housing challenge that comes their way, especially those of single parents who have fallen through the cracks.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: My cut is about how we can help financially burdened single working parents, be they divorced, widowed, unwed or those with incarcerated spouses, to allow them to consistently experience HDB as a compassionate and trusted guide in their difficult journey of finding stable housing for themselves again.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I will focus on four interventions that I believe can help.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I am not sure if that is because of the eligibility criteria.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: However, anecdotally, many single parents sell their matrimonial flat after their divorce, disqualifying them for the scheme.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister verify and update us on the take-up rate of the ASSIST scheme?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I hope he can also explain the underlying principle of why only applicants who sold their flat before the divorce need apply and whether this scheme can be expanded to include those who sold their flat after their divorce.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If both of them cannot agree on which one of them will get that privilege, only the parent with care and control of all the children can be exempted from the debarment period when buying a second subsidised HDB flat.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some of these lower-income divorcees ordered by the Courts to split the care and control of their children thus feel trapped in between the three-year debarment for HDB home ownership and also being denied rental housing options simply because they do not have care for all the children.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister share whether it is possible to lift the three-year debarment period for access to subsidised housing for financially-challenged divorcees with split care and control of children, especially those who do not have kin who can house them?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has recently made really encouraging strides in showing compassion towards the situation of unwed mothers, giving them equal maternity leave and access to Child Development Accounts (CDA).

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I have a special respect for single mothers who choose to take the hard road of raising a child on their own when they could have chosen to abort or abandon their child out of fear for their own future.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They have chosen an uncommon path and, in light of our low birth rates, I believe such mothers should be supported rather than penalised for choosing to take responsibility for raising their child.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, because unwed mothers and their children are not considered a family nucleus, they do not qualify for family housing grants and they may only purchase a flat under the Singles Scheme at 35 years old.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I know there is the current argument about how "Singapore is a conservative society that does not accept unmarried single-parent families." I would like to also present the observation that many conservatives also pride themselves on their reverence for the sanctity of life, loyalty to kin and protective care of the next generation, family-centred values that many single unwed mothers have shown, and they share as well, because of their decision to raise their child.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is possible that there is more support from conservatives from this angle than we think.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I am aware from stories on the ground that there have been exceptions made for certain single unwed mothers, but the successes seem to be credited to a mixture of arbitrary reasons, like individual stubborn insistence, Member of Parliament (MP) appeals, HDB discretion or diligent advocacy by a public servant or social worker.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, it is quite unclear to an inexperienced observer what is the best process for an unwed single mother to take if she feels she has a good case.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister share what would be the most recommended path for an unwed mother under 35 to take through the system to afford a house of her own?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: My fourth and final point is for HDB to consider prototyping a user experience journey based on the single parent trying to navigate the HDB system.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But it cannot be that access to housing comes down to who has the most sympathetic story or the most passionate advocate.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I am very sure that this is not the HDB or whole-of-Government way.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: That would be a most exciting piece of social innovation.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If we cannot consider helping the parent, then, surely, we should consider helping the child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, it cannot be easy to go through a divorce, especially when children are involved.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will help ensure that the children are not left homeless after the divorce is finalised, and ease the transition into the next chapter of their lives.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Making housing arrangements post-divorce is a challenge for the parties and usually contribute towards their acrimony.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If they have children, sometimes, parties fight over care and control as they feel that the party with the children stand a better chance of getting subsidised HDB housing upon their divorce.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Even if parties are amicable, it is often not easy to finalise the arrangements on their existing HDB flat as decisions on sale, transfer or retention of flats will have significant implications for both parties.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They will have to worry about issues of refunding of CPF monies to the other party if there is a transfer, getting a further HDB loan, finding a suitable new flat, debarment from rental and purchase of a new flat or paying the resale levy in the future.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These issues are not new and have been raised before and are being raised again here.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They also continue to be a perennial issue.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note that the Association of Women for Action and Research (AWARE) had also recently made recommendations on single parents' access to public housing based on findings from their research project.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At the Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS), I also see many divorcees who seek assistance on housing issues and make appeals to HDB.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In particular, I have met divorcees who do not have children or did not get care and control of their children and have difficulties finding housing after divorce.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note that, over the years, changes have been made to help alleviate difficulties faced by divorcees, especially those with children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For example, ASSIST was introduced to benefit second-timer divorced and widowed parents.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: HDB also exercises great flexibility in assisting individuals with difficulties in appropriate circumstances.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, could the Ministry do more to look into policies relating to housing for divorcees?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Could HDB also reconsider some of the rules in respect of debarment for rental or purchase of flat, housing loans and resale levies when the transaction for the flat arises from a Court order in a divorce?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They also represent an important safety net for the children of rental lessees or their next generation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I wish to take this opportunity to acknowledge the flexibility granted by HDB and the compassion extended to rental flat applicants for my MPS cases who narrowly missed the qualification criteria and to single mothers and divorced spouses in particular.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In this context, I have noted a small group of new rental flat applicants coming to my MPS with increasing frequency.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These are foreigners who were either married to Singaporeans in the past and who have Singaporean children or, separately, low wage-earning Singaporeans married to foreign spouses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As the rule stands today, neither group qualifies to apply for rental units and many are told of this when they visit HDB branch offices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More generally, the Government has reported a rise in the number of citizens marrying non-citizens.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While I recognise the limited number of rental units available for needy Singaporean families, the non-citizen spouses I spoke of earlier have a very close connection to Singapore by way of their children's place of birth or by way of marriage to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is some policy justification in favour of this by virtue of the non-citizen spouse scheme which recognises Singaporeans married to foreigners can buy an HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But I am just referring to the rental market right now.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope HDB would allow foreign spouses or ex-spouses to rent directly from HDB so as to allow the individuals concerned and their families to get back on their feet.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, please take your four cuts together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Which estates and flat types are most in demand?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How successful has the scheme been in encouraging married couples to have more children and as early as possible in their married lives?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How would the Ministry go about achieving this and what would be the steps taken to expedite the construction process?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Will additional costs be incurred in order to shorten the waiting time for the construction to be completed?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What is the total number of BTO flats that HDB intends to build ahead of the launches?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Would the Ministry also share how many flats for each room type will be built and where will the locations be?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Next, I would also like to ask how successful has the Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme (PPHS) been?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Can HDB lower the rental and allow the rental to be used to offset against the purchase price of the BTO flat?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Can the scheme be extended to couples still in the process of applying for flats?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Next, will HDB reconsider extending LBS to HDB flats other than 4-rooms and below?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: This would really enable many senior citizens to age in place.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: I would also like to appeal for the eligible age to be lowered and for approval to be granted for cases involving residents with special needs on compassionate grounds.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This can be a good thing, as our single seniors can provide company and support for one another.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There are many senior rental flat residents who experienced considerable difficulties in staying with their flatmates, usually resulting in bitter disputes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure many of our fellow Members have experienced that kind of appeals.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, it is often not easy for our HDB officers to help them find accommodation, either by helping these individuals to sometimes stay alone or by pairing them up with other seniors, and many of these are due to the shortage of rental flats.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Will HDB consider increasing the supply of rental flats by some amount so that there can be more room to accommodate seniors facing this issue?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In addition to this, this House was also informed that HDB conducts regular audits at different stages of construction to ensure compliance and quality control.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: While it may be good to know that HDB takes a no-nonsense approach to ensure the build quality of its projects, the reality on the ground can be a big letdown at times.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some of the designs and quality of BTO flats and upgrading projects I have encountered in Hougang are not acceptable.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The lift lobby lacks natural lighting in the daytime, which is a safety concern for senior citizens living there.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Were these potential design, safety and maintenance issues identified early, as mentioned by the Minister?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Does HDB expect the Town Councils to turn on the lights 24 hours a day at such lobbies to address the design concern?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Town Council also found undulating corridors due to poor workmanship, garden areas that do not have adequate sunlight, and designs that do not make sense.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: One such design is the sheltered linkway connecting Dewcourt to the older parts of the estate.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Instead of protecting residents from the rain, a few senior residents had fallen navigating that link as a result.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Lift Upgrading Programme (LUP) is another project with diverse designs and quality issues.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We have lift lobbies that are small to be effective and shelters that are not consistently applied across the estate.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Some blocks have them and some do not, for no apparent reasons.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Yet, some lift shafts are so well built that the Town Council has very little issue maintaining them.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, where and when do the assurance in quality and control come in?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Is the Town Council expected to do a thorough check for defects when it has neither control over the design nor oversight on the work progress and workmanship?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Is it even proper for HDB to hand over an incomplete project to the Town Council to maintain in the first place?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: While some of the issues I mentioned are being rectified at this moment, either by the contractors or Town Council, why are these issues not picked up during the regular audits at the different stages of construction, as highlighted by the Minister?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: A lot of time and effort were wasted trying to chase down contractors to make good the defects and design anomalies.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I have residents who asked me how did their BTO flats pass the Building and Construction Authority (BCA) in the first place.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It certainly has something to do with the design, inferior material used or ineffective quality control on the ground.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The comprehensive management system implemented by HDB to oversee its projects is all good but it must translate into acceptable results and quality on the ground consistently.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: My residents always tell me, "Sister Wah, I have lived here for 30 years and I am now old; my flat is also getting old, the wall tiles are falling off and the toilet bowl is almost broken.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Can you help us?" We can see that HIP is very important and everyone needs it.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: This is because there are many residents who have lived there from the start and would very much like to have a brand new flat, especially a new toilet.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: (In English): I would like to highlight another issue.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: A resident aged 50-plus told me that she has been trying for the first time and still not successful.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: So, perhaps, there is a shortage of 2-room flats.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These flats, for example, those flats in the constituency that I serve in Changi Simei have aged and do need essential upgrading, such as repairing of spalling concrete and structural cracks, replacement of waste and soil discharge stacks, replacement of pipe sockets and new clothes drying racks.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While we understand that upgrading is a major expenditure, but these upgrading works are essential due to the age of the flats and for the safety of residents.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: To nurture a distinctively Singaporean and inclusive home for the people who may need a little help with mobility, the elderly, the disabled, key facilities and amenities must be distributed nearer to homes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Our vision is to move towards a smart city, which should make it easier to facilitate barrier-free accessibility and greater travel convenience.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But we should not only be reliant on the physical aspects to create an inclusive, well-connected city.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: New innovative growth centres just outside the downtown area as well as innovative work arrangements are just some examples of how we can better connect everyone in other aspects of living.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Next, I want to talk quickly about the price of public housing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The Government has introduced cooling measures to bring down housing prices from an absurdly high level.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: They have worked somewhat, but it is undeniable that HDB flats are expensive and out of reach for some, especially young couples who have only just started working and do not have much savings.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Back when HDB was trying to encourage home ownership, Singaporeans were less affluent, but many could contribute to the nation's vision of a home for everyone.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Most of these home owners have already paid off their loans and are debt-free.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Singaporeans are more affluent these days, but housing prices have rocketed and the younger generation feels enslaved by debts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Maybe we need to reintegrate the principles of public housing which some have perceived have diminished slightly, even the perceived view that HDB prices are being commercialised.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a testament to Singapore's abilities to develop, attract and retain talent.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Committee on the Future Economy's (CFE's) recommended strategy of developing a vibrant and connected city of opportunity further homes in on the point that it is important for us to be well-connected externally and rejuvenate our internal landscape over time to attract talent and support economic growth and development for our citizens.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore's progressive and forward-thinking attitude towards urban rejuvenation has helped us to avoid the problem of urban decay that many major cities in the region are now facing.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One example of how urban planning can be aligned with growth strategies to spur economic development is the transformation of the Marina Bay area.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With integrative planning, the Marina Bay area has been transformed from mudflats and empty plots of reclaimed land into a vibrant financial and service hub that combines both work and recreation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The challenge that we now face is this: how can we continue to plan boldly and more integratively to attract talent not only for our citizens' benefit and attract this elusive "creative-class" that, according to the University of Toronto's Prof Richard Florida, will drive economic growth in an increasingly talent-starved world?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the CFE's recommendations is to create new spaces underground.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While Singapore has already begun to explore this option with MINDEF's underground ammo storage and Kim Chuan depot, the largest underground train depot in the world, would this also be a viable and sustainable housing option?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If the answer is yes, how will this impact our way of living?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Sin is from the Pioneer Generation and his wife is 66 years old this year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They used to live in cramped conditions in a rented flat in a Chinatown shophouse.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When HDB started the Homeownership for the People Scheme in 1964, they were among the first to sign up for a 3-room flat in Havelock Road.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The flat gave them a home to call their own and a concrete stake in the wealth of the nation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They stayed there in the same home for almost 50 years, brought up two children who are now married and have their own families.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Last year, Mr and Mrs Sin decided to right-size to a 2-room flexi-flat near their second child.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They converted some of their home equity into cash and CPF savings.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They are financially independent and they can now enjoy their golden years with their two grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is the Singapore Dream, HDB-style, and their story is not unique.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am sure many of us can relate to this in our lives or that of our parents or we would have met many residents like them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While we have achieved tremendous success with home ownership, I recognise that Singaporeans are still concerned about the future.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is reflected in the speeches of many Members during the Budget Debate and I have also met many parents who worried about their children's future as well as young Singaporeans who ask me whether they can look forward to a better life than their parents had.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I understand these concerns and they are not unique to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Enabling home ownership is a major challenge in cities everywhere.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Young people struggle with high living expenses and home prices.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, I read a recent report of the situation in the UK.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In 1998, it took an average worker about three years to afford the downpayment to buy a home in the UK.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Today, it takes 20 years − from three to 20 today.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As a result, many young people in the UK have no chance of buying a property.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our situation in Singapore is very different from the UK and other countries and this did not happen by chance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is because we made home ownership a strategic priority from the start of nation-building and have continually invested in it over the decades, a point which Mr Alex Yam and many other Members of this House made earlier.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why couples are today assured of a quality home at an affordable price even before they get married, something that no other country in the world can offer.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are committed to keeping this Singapore dream alive − to help couples secure their flats more quickly, start their families, sink roots into the community and have a concrete stake in our nation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As Mr Gan Thiam Poh highlighted just now, first-timer married couples with or expecting a child already enjoy priority under the Parenthood Priority Scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As with many other first-timer families, mature estates and larger flat types are popular with such applicants.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I would encourage them to apply in the non-mature estates, where nine in 10 applicants of BTO flats are successful.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, if you are a first-timer applying for a BTO flat in non-mature estates, you can book one within the year, unless you insist on choosing a specific town or location.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, if you apply for a flat in a non-mature estate today, the waiting time comprises mostly of the construction time of about three to four years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In addition, we will launch these projects with special quotas to further prioritise young couples who are ready to settle down.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These flat types are the most popular amongst first-timer families.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The quotas for smaller flat types will remain unchanged to meet the housing needs of second-timers, singles and the elderly who right-size.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Besides BTO, our Sale of Balance Flats (SBF) exercises are also a popular option for couples who wish to get their new flats quickly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Due to their large scale and variety, balance flats are currently only offered twice a year and applicants will apply for a specific town and the flat type.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But there are some balance flats left unsold after each SBF exercise.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Each time we put out an SBF exercise twice a year, there will still be flats that are left unsold.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I have asked HDB to offer these unsold flats for sale in a more efficient manner.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Instead of releasing these unsold flats by specific towns and flat types, we will pool together unsold units and put them out for balloting at more regular intervals.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then, those with urgent housing needs and who are less particular about location can apply and need not wait for the usual SBF exercise which only happens twice a year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This will be a new sales mode with balloting priority given to first-timers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: HDB will launch the first such exercise in the latter half of this year and will announce more details when ready.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Regardless of how long the waiting time is, as highlighted by Mr Gan Thiam Poh, PPHS allows couples to start building a life together while waiting for their flat to be completed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: One such couple is Mr and Mrs Leong.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They booked a BTO flat in 2013, and then while waiting, they moved into a PPHS flat in Dover Road with their three-month old daughter.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While they were there, they welcomed the arrival of not just one, but two other daughters while staying in the PPHS flat.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Their new 4-room BTO flat in Keat Hong is ready, and the family of five will be moving in soon.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I think Ms Josephine Teo and the National Population and Talent Division (NPTD) office will be very happy with what we are doing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We know that every dollar counts for a young family just starting out.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why HDB rents out PPHS flats at subsidised rates.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Darryl David and several Members have asked whether we can lower the rents even more.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This will give young couples more affordable options to start their lives together while waiting for their new flats to be completed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Ms Tin Pei Ling also suggested making available PPHS flats to couples who are still applying for BTO flats, meaning to say, their flats have not been booked yet, but they are still in the process of applying.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We can study this but let us remember that PPHS rentals are highly subsidised, so it is fair that we set clear timelines for the couples to stay in PPHS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The best way to ensure this is when they have already booked a flat, and then we know that the flat is booked and there is a specific timeline for which they need the PPHS rentals.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And there are many more options to choose from in the resale market.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We know that affordability can still be a concern for such young couples, especially when they are just starting out.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why we have increased the grants for resale flats, as announced in the Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: With the enhanced grants, most young couples should be able to afford the downpayment for their resale flats.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Alex Yam and Assoc Prof Randolph Tan asked if the enhanced CPF Housing Grant will push up resale prices.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are aware of this risk and have studied the matter very carefully.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we expect resale prices to remain stable for a few reasons.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A good number of owners will be selling their existing flats when they move into their newly completed homes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that additional supply will help to soak up the increase in demand.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Moreover, sellers will need to be realistic in pricing their flats because home buyers always have the option to buy a new flat from HDB.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that puts some reality check on the prices that sellers would be able to set.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The resale price is also linked to the overall state of the property market.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah suggested removing the ABSD for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Several other Members have mentioned this on previous occasions as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The property measures have helped to achieve a soft landing in prices.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Today, housing demand remains firm, given the current interest rate environment and income growth.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we will continue to monitor this carefully to maintain a stable and sustainable property market.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing had at the Budget Debate suggested reviewing the concept of ownership of residential properties, such that if a residential property is held by a corporate entity or a special purpose vehicle, and the shares of the company are transferred from seller to buyer, the normal residential stamp duty should apply.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In principle, we should treat transactions in residential property on the same basis, regardless of whether the property is transferred directly or through a transfer of shares in a company whose primary business is in residential property in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we plan to make legislative changes to effect this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The aim or the intent is not to impact the ordinary buying and selling of shares in such companies when they are listed on the stock market by retail investors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: However, significant owners of residential property holding entities will be subject to the usual stamp duties when they transfer equity interest in such entities, like what would happen if they were to buy or sell the property directly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: With the changes in CPF grants, let us take a look at how a resale HDB flat compares against the BTO options today.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Let us take the example of a couple looking to settle down in their first home together and looking to buy a place near their parents in Tampines, a mature estate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The price of a 4-room new flat in Tampines is about $300,000 to $360,000.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A 4-room resale flat in Tampines is now selling for about $430,000, before grants.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: With the grants, the resale flat price will be comparable to a new flat price.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, a young couple looking for a flat in Tampines can buy a resale flat and move in immediately.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will do one more enhancement for the resale market, and before Members get excited, let me assure Members that it has nothing to do with price or grants, but we are going to do something for the transaction process.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we can leverage technology and make the process faster and more streamlined.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I hope that all these measures will make housing more affordable and accessible for young couples and help them to start their marriage and parenthood journey early.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At the same time, I encourage young couples to do your research and consider the different housing options.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Be prudent and find a place that is within your budget and means.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If you are looking for resale, choose a flat with a sufficiently long lease to cover your needs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then, like Mr and Mrs Sin, you will have a home and a nest-egg that you can tap on for retirement later in life.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While our focus is on helping first-timers, HDB flats also meet the housing needs of Singaporeans at every life stage.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our family, job and financial circumstances change over the course of our lives.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The housing arrangement that was suitable when we were young may no longer be the right fit some years down the road.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For those who come back to HDB again as second-timers, we are helping them with a number of measures that we have introduced or enhanced in the past few years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, some may wish to move closer to family members after their grandchildren are born, or as the grandparents age, for mutual care and support.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These families can benefit from the enhanced Married Child Priority Scheme (MCPS), the Multi-Generation Priority Scheme (MGPS), or 3Gen flats if they are buying new flats; or they can benefit from the Proximity Housing Grant (PHG) for resale flats which we introduced earlier.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are also providing more housing options for singles.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will continue to put out more 2-room BTO flats to meet the needs of singles.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Singles can also opt for a resale flat and benefit from the enhanced CPF Housing Grant announced in this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, for a first-timer single buying a resale flat under the Single Singapore Citizen (SSC) Scheme can now qualify for the CPF Housing Grant of $25,000 for a 4-room or smaller flat, or $20,000 for a 5-room flat.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Eligible singles applying under the Joint Singles Scheme (JSS) will receive the CPF Housing Grant of the same amount as first-timer families.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Several Members − Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin, Mr Louis Ng, Ms Rahayu Mahzam and Miss Cheryl Chan − also asked about how we are helping vulnerable groups, including divorcees and single unwed parents.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are fully committed to helping them with their housing needs and making sure no one falls through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If they are unable to afford a flat and do not have alternative housing options, HDB will assist them with a rental flat, and we are continuing to build more rental flats to meet these needs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In the last three years, HDB has helped nearly 2,000 single parents with a public rental flat.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And by single parents, we mean divorcees with children as well as unwed mothers with children.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is about 27% of all households who were allocated a public rental flat during that time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Every case that HDB receives is unique and our officers will review each case very carefully.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If necessary, they will work together with the local social service agencies − the SSOs, the Family Service Centre social workers − to assess the family's situation and they will exercise flexibility for those in difficulties.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Besides helping with rental, we also introduced the Fresh Start Housing Scheme last year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This was to provide additional grants for second-timer families living in rental flats, so that they can purchase their own homes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Saktiandi mentioned this and asked about the status.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have just opened up for applications in December and I recently visited some of the families who applied for the scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: One of them is a single mother who moved into her rental flat a few years ago, together with her daughter who just entered secondary school.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They are getting support from various parties, including from the family.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The grandmother helps to look after the daughter after school so that the mother can work.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is an aunt who takes her daughter to the library because she enjoys reading.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) officers who check-in with them regularly to see how they are doing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it shows that this is not just about getting a flat, as important as that is.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is about the family having all-round support which the Government and the community can provide.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is what we are doing with Fresh Start.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In this case, the family will be applying for a new 2-room flexi flat by the end of the year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are very happy for them and we wish them all the best in their Fresh Start journey.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I have shared broadly our approach in helping these vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will elaborate further and give more updates on the progress of the Fresh Start scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Another important group that we watch out for is our seniors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They have a nest egg in their HDB flats and many would like to tap into this nest egg so that they can live out their golden years comfortably.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Today, seniors who wish to monetise their flat can consider a range of options.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They can rent out a room, they can apply for LBS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Zainal Sapari suggested extending LBS in various ways.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have also extended the LBS to 4-room flats to cover the majority of seniors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For those in larger flats, it is better to tap on other monetisation options, such as right-sizing to a smaller flat.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I want to dwell a bit on what we want to do to make right-sizing more attractive.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are providing more options for seniors to do so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why we introduced the 2-room flexi scheme, with flexibility on the choice of lease length, the flat size and internal fittings.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are building more of these 2-room flexi flats and setting aside supply of such flats specially for seniors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are also offering priority to those moving near their existing flat or near their married children.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we are seeing better success rates for seniors who are applying for these 2-room flexi flats.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Currently, the numbers who take up the right-sizing option are not large.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When we survey and ask people, they tell us that the process is sometimes quite daunting.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we will work at making the entire process of right-sizing much easier through three moves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, we will introduce more hand-holding for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Seniors who are interested in exploring their monetisation options can walk-in to the HDB Hub or branches and receive one-on-one financial consultation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: To make their experience more comfortable, we have implemented an elderly priority queue at the HDB Hub so that they can get prompt attention and our officers will guide them through the right-sizing process.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Second, we will allow right-sizing seniors to defer the full downpayment until key collection.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This will be a big help to the seniors who are right-sizing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Third, we will introduce a new Temporary Loan to help those with cash flow issues at the key collection stage.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Currently, those who are right-sizing can make use of the HDB cash contra facility.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What this means is that when you sell your existing flat and you buy a new one, you can contra.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But this requires some coordination in timing because you complete the sale of the existing flat and collect the keys to your new flat on the same day as a back-to-back transaction.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: While we have seniors in mind, we will extend the Temporary Loan to our non-elderly who need this, so that a wider group of home buyers can benefit as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we have these three moves that we hope will make right-sizing more convenient, more accessible for all our seniors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We hope that this tailored package of measures will make the whole right-sizing process a more pleasant one for our seniors, from start to finish.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is something that we have always been very mindful of.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What we enjoy today is the result of long-term commitment, meticulous planning and painstaking implementation, year by year, decade after decade.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why, today, we have beautiful HDB homes set in lush greenery and waters, like what you see here in Tengah Forest Town where we are going to put up the first batch of flats by next year.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I note what Mr Png Eng Huat said earlier about quality issues and defects.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I will be the first to admit that HDB is not perfect.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In all building projects, there will always be some defects here and there, and that is why there is a period where the developer will come in to remedy the defects.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I would say, let us be fair and objective in assessing HDB's quality over the years and decades.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Any objective assessment of the quality of HDB's projects would show that the quality has, indeed, improved.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If you look at independent scoring of quality, like the CONQUAS score, which measures construction quality, indeed, they have improved over the years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And whenever we see that there are defects or issues, we will make sure that HDB goes in to remedy them and put things right.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And if there are specifics in the case of what Mr Png had mentioned, we will look at them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are doing this in our HDB estates to make them more beautiful, to make them more inclusive as well, so that we have an inclusive environment for people of all ages and abilities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are building a more vibrant town with its own distinctive character, heritage and identity − attributes that Mr Alex Yam mentioned.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are also building more integrated mixed-use districts where people can live, work and play together.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are also taking steps to rejuvenate our older estates.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it is not just about new towns, but we are also taking steps to rejuvenate the older ones.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I note the suggestions by Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Ms Jessica Tan to extend the HIP.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I have explained before our position on this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have undertaken upgrading projects before and we will continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We need to replace existing infrastructure assets which are ageing and also invest in new infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Members already know about our plans to expand Changi Airport and Tuas Terminal.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we have other infrastructure needs, too, including in our public transport system, our utilities system like water − which we had discussed extensively in the Budget Debate − sewage, waste, our power grids.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: All these are crucial in enabling economic growth, generating jobs and improving the quality of life for our people.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We cannot assume that all new infrastructure will be automatically put in place and old ones will be automatically upgraded by the Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Look at the situation in many first-world democracies where infrastructure is deteriorating.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Just take America as an example where some cities are literally still relying on water and sewage pipelines that were built more than a century ago.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Partly because of "Not in my back yard" (NIMBY) mindsets and opposition from various interest groups, because it is not in my backyard, I oppose a new infrastructure next to my home.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is partly also because infrastructure projects are very expensive and many governments do not have the resources to fund them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because of all these difficulties, there is a tendency for politicians to kick the infrastructure can down the road and focus on short-term deliverables.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why you see the situation you see in many advanced developed countries − infrastructure gets neglected and the result is deteriorating infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are not immune to these pressures, so we must never assume that infrastructure will automatically get done in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If the economy fails, if there are no fiscal resources, if there is an incompetent government, then nothing will happen and infrastructure will stagnate and Singapore will decline.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Some people have also asked me if there is a lot more we can do, given our land constraints.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: What more can we do in Singapore where everything is already developed?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the fact is that we have yet to reach our physical limits.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are exploring ways to expand space options, including underground space, as Mr Darryl David mentioned just now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And underground space is not so much for underground living.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I do not think we are ready for that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we can certainly put utilities and storage facilities and many other things underground.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then, valuable surface land can be freed up for housing, greenery and other uses.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, there is tremendous potential to dream big, think boldly and build a new Singapore for the next 50 years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We must not let complacency set in or, worse, allow a culture of stasis to take root and ossify our society.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The same spirit of innovation that we need for the economy must be applied to planning our future city and home.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We must find innovative ways to build new infrastructure for the future.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We must develop new and innovative urban concepts that will make Singapore a more attractive, sustainable and liveable home.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Take the example of how we have succeeded in building a Garden City.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Some of you would have read the recent reports of how Singapore was ranked as the city with the highest density of trees worldwide.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is a result of decades of hard work, with a strong personal push and commitment by our founding Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But now that we are where we are today, what comes after this?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Is this the climax of all that we need to do?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, our next phase is to be a City in a Garden.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And this is not just a slogan or a clever turn of phrase.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We must continue to enhance our greenery further, not just at the ground level, but even sky-rise level.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We must enhance our biodiversity and learn to live in harmony with nature, the flora and fauna around us for all to enjoy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Likewise, on economic infrastructure, we are known for good economic infrastructure, which attracts companies from around the world.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But we cannot afford to stand still while others catch up and move ahead.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, how can we invest in new infrastructure to make Singapore even more competitive, attract more investments and create more jobs for our people?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: CFE had studied this and set out several recommendations, as several Members have also highlighted.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our aim is to create new growth centres not just in the downtown area, but all over our island.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And these new centres can be nodes for related industry clusters to come together, including in new growth areas like FinTech and cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will also set up more innovation spaces for incubators, accelerators and startups.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This was something that Mr Liang Eng Hwa had suggested earlier in the Budget Debate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These new centres will be attractive spaces for Singaporeans to live, work and play together.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is no ordinary site because when we consulted with many experts, including experts from abroad, they have told us that it is very rare to find such a site in other cities, which is located in a setting of lush greenery and water, the way we have in Jurong Lake District now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we will integrate our new developments with the surrounding greenery and water bodies in Jurong Lake Gardens which, itself, is being enhanced and revamped as our new National Gardens in the west.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This will be a beautiful new setting for waterfront housing and office spaces.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When we complete the High-Speed Rail Station, it will not only be a major transport node connected to our Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) lines but will also have a central linear park on the surface, connecting to Jurong Lake Gardens.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This will not just be a second CBD.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But it has the potential to be a centre with multiple dimensions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The High-Speed Rail Station will make Jurong Lake District a new gateway to Singapore and a regional hub for ASEAN businesses.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Jurong Lake District is near the new Tuas Terminal that we are building in the west.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is a mixed-use area comprising residential land uses, the new Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) campus and also commercial and business park users.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, we will appoint a Master Developer for the whole district and allow more flexible land use within the area.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: JTC will then have the flexibility to develop the district based on land use and gross plot ratio guidelines at the overall district level.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In other words, instead of having planning controls imposed on individual land parcels, JTC will be able to optimise land use across the entire development and find ways to integrate the needs of different users.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, since SIT's campus and the JTC's business parks are located side by side, we can have closer integration of the facilities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: SIT's research labs, incubator spaces and learning facilities can be located inside JTC business park buildings and shared with the industry.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At the same time, SIT can host industry research and development facilities and startup spaces within their buildings.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This will help to create synergies between students and businesses, between academia and businesses, facilitate test-bedding and prototyping of new innovations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The second benefit of having such a master developer is that it can help to more comprehensively design and implement good pedestrian connectivity and public spaces.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Traditionally, a desired network of public spaces and connectivity links can only be realised over a long period of time as the various land parcels are developed step by step.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: With a master developer overseeing the implementation of an enterprise district, the key pedestrian routes and public spaces can be identified upfront and a more comprehensive network can be implemented.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Thirdly, the master developer will plan for and implement district-wide systems like district cooling, pneumatic waste conveyance system to support the district, all of which will help to reduce energy usage and enhance the sustainability and attractiveness of the environment.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The whole precinct is about 17 hectares in size.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The traditional approach would be to carve it out and put out individual plots for sale.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But this time, we will tender out the entire site for a master developer.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will give flexibility for the master developer to come up with the overall plan and develop the project by phases, in line with market demand.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the master developer will also have to be responsible for certain outcomes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Along the way, we will enhance the river with more greenery, seamless jogging and cycling paths.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are many more that are being worked on.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These are major moves that will take decades to complete and the Government cannot do this work alone.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
