text: We will need close partnerships with the community and private sector and the collective efforts of all to develop new innovative urban solutions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I call on Singaporeans to join us in this exciting journey to build and remake our entire city.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The best cities in the world are defined not by their buildings or infrastructure, but by their people − it is the spirit and imagination, the culture and identity of our people.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we must be prepared to adapt to change and constantly innovate and improve.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We must continue to embrace diversity and welcome new ideas and talent.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We must be prepared to work hard and make sacrifices today so that we can reap the fruits tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is what our Pioneers did for us; and that is how we can, in turn, pay it forward for our next generation − a greater city, an endearing home, a better Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development and Ministers for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Since its inception, MSO seems to have grown in its engagements with other agencies and types of issues it helps to address.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We take great pride in the fact that our municipal services function well and are generally up to the task of meeting the high standards that we Singaporeans set for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: MSO was set up two years ago precisely to improve upon such service delivery.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With the myriad of Government agencies that participate in providing municipal services, it is not surprising that members of the public could easily get confused about which three-letter acronym to call when they are in trouble.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Within my own constituency, I am grateful to MSO for facilitating residents' feedback and organising joint action by different agencies.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There was this case where MSO was involving the Agri-Food and Veterinary Authority (AVA), the National Environment Agency (NEA), HDB and Town Council to resolve a resident's complaint about a group of 50 bird enthusiasts who were using the linkhouse in front of a resident's flat to train parrots.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And the second case involved a resident playing saxophone in a public park in the evenings which affected the peace of the surrounding flats.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Unfortunately, this fell outside the purview of Town Council, HDB, NEA and the Police.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: At this juncture, I would like to ask MSO to provide an update on the overall progress that it has made, especially over the past year.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can MSO provide some specific examples of initiatives that have taken place in tandem with the Town Councils to the benefit of residents?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Last but not least, MSO has sought to leverage the prevalence of information and communications technology (ICT), such as cellphones, among Singaporeans.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Chairman, can I take the three cuts together?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: All of these agencies, and I would like to acknowledge each of them: AVA, BCA, HDB, Land Transport Authority (LTA), NEA, NParks, PA, Public Utilities Board (PUB), Singapore Land Authority (SLA), Singapore Police Force (SPF) and URA − not all of them have three-letter acronyms, by the way − all of them work very hard and, most of the time, tirelessly behind the scene so that we in Singapore can enjoy one of the world's highest quality living environments.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: The beauty and strength of Singapore's Public Service is that every agency has a clear focus and has built the expertise to perform its role well.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Hence, the potential of MSO should be more than the strength of the 11 agencies or, if we include MSO, more than the strength of 12 agencies.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: The sum should be greater than the parts.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Singapore may be an urban jungle but we do have a lot of wildlife here: mynahs and pigeons.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Their numbers have increased tremendously because of the easy access to food.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: One would assume that the birds would, therefore, only congregate at hawker centres and coffee shops, but no.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: In Tampines, I receive feedback from residents that their laundry has been soiled by bird droppings, and some even have birds flying into their flats.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: And these areas do not have food establishments nearby.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: I am sure this happens at other estates as well.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: The reason why the birds would gather at these areas is because there are people feeding them.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: People would throw bread, rice or other food either out of the kitchen window or onto the ground.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: I even know of an elderly man who would carry a backpack full of birdfeed.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: He would grab a handful, stretch out his hand and let birds feed from his hand.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: You can literally see birds flying around him as he walks around the estate.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: So, I call him the Snow White of Tampines.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: However, both agencies can only apprehend the culprit when caught red-handed.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: But throwing out of the window is just a fleeting action.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Usually, the Town Council will just have to clean up the leftover food, the bird droppings and the bird feathers.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: However, I am sure there will be a lot of public feedback to AVA, NEA or Town Council through email, telephone or through the MSO app.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: If we are able to consolidate the data, we would have a better sense of where and when the feeder strikes and maybe even who the feeder is.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: It does not need to be very sophisticated or hi-tech methods.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Sometimes, residents or the cleaners themselves can offer invaluable information, just that there is no one lead agency talking to them, trying to piece together the various pieces of information or data, making sense of it and solving the problem.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: This approach can also be applied to issues of irresponsible cat feeding, high-rise littering and noise nuisances.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Chairman, Harvard professors Stephen Goldsmith and Susan Crawford wrote a book, "The Responsive City: Engaging Communities Through Data-Smart Governance".

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: According to them, a "responsive" city is one that does not just make ordinary transactions like making paying a parking ticket easier, but one that uses the information generated by its interactions with residents to better understand and predict the needs of neighbourhoods, to measure the effectiveness of city agencies and workers, to identify waste and fraud, to increase transparency and, most importantly, to solve problems.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: By using its own data and social media, a city "should learn what its citizens are saying about their needs and the issues in their communities.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: It should learn across agencies about the solutions to problems; it should learn from the data about good actors and bad actors.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: The way most governments are organised tend to focus on specific key performance indicators (KPIs) and some people would call it the silo-ed nature of public services, often pointed to as a factor behind inefficiency or poor outcomes.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: However, our public agencies are not doing shoddy work.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: But because they are specialised agencies handling specific problems, there is a greater need for better coordination, closer collaboration and integrated solutions.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: When responsibilities fall onto different agencies which does not work in an integrated way, opportunities to intervene earlier or more effectively are missed.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: For transactional or back office services, a lack of integration will lead to duplicated activity and poor services experienced by residents, such as having to provide the same information over and over again.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: This problem of silo-ed working can apply to data as well, as silos extend to the data they hold, making it difficult for services to view data held by other agencies.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: This is a huge missed opportunity as, in recent years, the power of linked and integrated data to provide insight into complex phenomena has become more apparent.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Typically, concerns about the legality of data sharing and information governance have prevented the creation of large, linked datasets across public services.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Linked data is effectively the creation of an online information architecture, sometimes referred to as data warehousing.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: It offers the ability to access data involved through an online portal.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Under the impetus of the Smart Nation initiative, I hope that MSO would also develop a vision where technology could be adopted to improve municipal service delivery, and consolidated data could be better used for improvements to operations and service delivery.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, can you allow Minister Grace Fu to answer?

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: MSO takes a people-centric focus in bringing about better municipal services.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We work with agencies to streamline processes for complex or cross-cutting municipal issues.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In the short two years, we have undertaken many initiatives towards this goal.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon and Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal have asked for an update.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: One of our first initiatives was the OneService app, which made it easier for residents to provide feedback on municipal matters without the need to search for the right agency.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have received many compliments from residents, who complimented agencies on their prompt responses and for taking residents' feedback seriously.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Going forward, in line with the direction of the Smart Nation initiative, we want to expand the app from a feedback tool to a multi-channel network that connects the Government, the people and the private sector with one another.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The first crowdsourcing feature in the app is called "Spot Abandoned Trolleys", and was introduced in April last year, which attracted over 4,600 reported cases.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Last September, MSO launched the OneService Portal to complement the app, where residents can access information on services and updates in their neighbourhood.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Recently, MSO also released a municipal case map on both platforms which show all feedback received by Government agencies over the past seven days.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Users can see all the cases reported on their neighbourhood.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Besides improving the interface with the public, MSO paid attention to streamlining processes that involve multiple agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For instance, LTA was appointed as the First Responder for feedback on maintenance of connectivity-related infrastructure.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our efforts have paid off and agencies are increasingly taking on a collaborative approach in handling interagency issues.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For example, LTA received feedback last year from a concerned Mdm Ngeo on some uneven metal steps and a sunken manhole near a road junction.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: LTA approached PUB as the steps were on top of a drain.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In view of public safety, PUB carried out repair works promptly.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Concurrently, LTA reached out to Singtel which helped trace the sunken manhole to NetLink Trust, thereby facilitating rectification works.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: LTA and PUB staff had taken upon themselves to go beyond their job scope − LTA in proactively reaching out to relevant parties for follow-up, PUB in moving in to rectify the issue in a timely manner.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: If they had not done so, MSO would not know better as an additional day or two taken would not affect their KPIs.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is just one of many cases that they handle on a daily basis.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But it is because of what they did and collectively with other officers in our partner agencies, handling frontline customer services, carrying out operations on the ground, carrying out maintenance and rectification works, that we see a steady improvement in service delivery since MSO's formation.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: MSO also strengthened our partnership with the Town Councils, which play a key role in municipal service delivery in HDB estates.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have embarked on a number of initiatives together.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Then, we moved on to streamlining operations on the ground and establishing Standard Operating Protocols, such as the one for water issues between PUB and Town Councils.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This means that public feedback can now be transferred seamlessly between agencies and Town Councils via the systems, thus ensuring proper follow-up.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: MSO has also conducted a series of Learning Journeys, where representatives from Town Councils and Government agencies were brought together for learning.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This fostered a better understanding of each other's work and resulted in better alignment of the work processes and information-sharing for issues like high-rise littering which Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal and Mr Baey Yam Keng mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Indeed, in one of the sessions we had with NEA, the Town Council participants found it useful to learn how NEA deploys its cameras to capture high-rise littering offences, as well as some of NEA's operational challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The coordination between the Town Council and NEA in addressing high-rise littering has improved as a result.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Given the positive response, MSO is planning to expand the Learning Journeys to involve more agencies and Town Council officers.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As we continue to facilitate more collaborations between our partner agencies and Town Councils, we want to expand our role to an enabler, one which equips our agencies and Town Councils with tools to be more productive.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is particularly critical in view of the tightening labour market and technological disruptions.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Municipal service delivery will need to adapt and take advantage of new technologies to be better and more efficient.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Many of MSO's partner agencies have already started to leverage technology for service delivery.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For example, SLA and the Government Technology Agency (GovTech) have successfully completed a Proof of Concept on the use of drones and video analytics to automatically detect defects on state properties and land.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This fund will be channeled towards the development of technological initiatives by our partner agencies to enhance productivity in municipal services.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In this regard, MSO plays the role of a coordinator and facilitator.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We facilitate the participation of the relevant agencies, coordinate efforts and remove roadblocks to projects that cut across different agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We also aim to promote the application of one agency's technology in other areas so that we can achieve greater benefit from technology use.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This allows the contractor to check his work against prescribed standards and perform rectification works if necessary before leaving the site.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: NParks officers can monitor the contractors' work remotely, thus reducing the need for physical inspection.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A better outcome for grass-cutting is achieved with fewer man-hours required.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We look forward to working with the private sector, including SMEs, in commercialising the sensor.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We hope to help our partner agencies to develop an innovative idea into a workable solution and enable the private sector to participate in the innovation.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Good municipal services should go beyond merely responding quickly to feedback.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Managing municipal issues upstream and anticipating operational requirements can better address public concerns.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We agree with Mr Baey Yam Keng that integrated data has great potential in this aspect.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As a start, we have leveraged our integrated feedback management system to study data received across agencies to better identify the location, timing and the cause of key issues.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We can deep dive into these hotspots to identify the root causes and devise holistic measures to address them.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: An example that I would like to quote through our data analytics is a strong correlation that we have identified between incidents of stray dogs reported with the start of construction sites.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our analysis has shown that the clearance of forested land, which precedes construction, would drive dogs out of their habitat, and food waste from construction sites might be a source of food for the dogs.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: AVA also worked with their Animal Welfare Group (AWG) partners to rehome suitable trapped dogs.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We also developed the Municipal Services Dashboard with GovTech, which allows Government and Town Councils to access visual representations of a whole range of cases by location, time, block and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This allows them to view patterns and trends which, in turn, give them useful information for operations planning.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: With better planning in terms of timing and frequency, our agencies can provide comprehensive, responsive and effective municipal services.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Going forward, apart from feedback data and in line with what Mr Baey said, MSO will also be working with agencies to facilitate other kinds of data sharing, such as camera footages, to improve the resolution of municipal issues.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: What we hope to achieve is, in fact, a deeper, cultural transformation to change how agencies work and how they collaborate with one another.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We want to create a work environment where agencies feel supported to explore new ways of doing things and try out new technologies, a culture where openness and empathy is the norm, a system where different parts of the Government work well together and collaborate with the private sector and the community.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And at the heart of our work is our many officers who believe in providing good efficient services to the public, officers who take pride in their work, go the extra mile in serving the public, and serving with honour.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Since my involvement with MSO, I have been consistently impressed by the enthusiasm and positive attitudes taken by the officers of our partner agencies who needed little persuasion to work towards the goals of MSO.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Once constraints, such as inter-organisational boundaries and limitations in resources were alleviated with our help, the staff quickly adjusted their work process on the ground and took up their new responsibilities willingly and with urgency.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I have received many compliments from different people on the prompt and thorough follow-ups by agency officers.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Hence, I would like to record my gratitude to all the staff of our agencies for their positive attitude and service to the public.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We in MSO can do what we do only because of their cooperation and dedication.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Out of these, how many new projects will be under the Ministry?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What would be the total valuation of these projects and what specific initiatives will MND inject into the market to help our contractors?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Our construction sector is in dire need of stimulation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Our local contractors are losing business to foreign contractors, some of whom can provide cheaper raw materials and labour from their home countries while some have more impressive track records and support from their parent companies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: I know that in some cases, the Government is breaking up large projects into parcels to enable local contractors to participate.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Certainly, I agree that more innovative ideas are needed to boost productivity.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Why are our contractors not so keen to embrace new technologies?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Many said they may not be able to get sufficient projects to recover their investment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Perhaps, the Government can have some schemes for them that ensure them of the volume of projects should they invest in new technology.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Concrete Prefabricated Prefinished Volumetric Construction (PPVC) is one but not the only one.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Steel construction could be equally productive if we know the know-how.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Besides that, giving more time in upfront planning and design can go a long way in saving resources and time.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: In Singapore, very often, the moment the developer gets the land, he would want to rush the design submission so that he can launch his project for sale as soon as possible.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Architects and engineers are building Building Information Modelling (BIM) models just good enough for submission and get approval.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Later, when the contractor comes on board, he builds his own BIM model.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Where is the benefit that BIM is supposed to bring to the team?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: For the HDB's Early Contractor Involvement (ECI), I was told that four to five teams of contractors are called in.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Is it not a waste of time and resources?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: I hope that the Government, being the largest developer in Singapore, can lead by example.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: The Ministry should help them to build up track records and get them on board government-to-government (G-to-G) projects overseas.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Singapore can benefit from a more resilient, reputable and capable construction industry with in-house local competency.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: HUDC estates are an integral part of the HDB towns.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: Many common areas, facilities, footpaths and road access are shared by residents living in both estates.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: More thought has to be put into estate planning post-privatisation or else such issues will surface.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: There is no way to access Block 712 Hougang Avenue 2 from Hougang Avenue 2.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: Calling a taxi, ordering a delivery or having friends over for a party requires precise directions to be given.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: Over at Hougang Avenue 7, a whole new set of issues surfaced after the fencing of the privatised HUDC estate went up.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: Residents living in the surrounding HDB estate no longer have a safe passage to the main road.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: Residents are forced to walk on the fringe of the fencing or on the service road to get to Hougang Avenue 7.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: It gets more challenging for residents on wheelchairs or with baby prams as they have to navigate a narrow zig-zag two-way traffic road.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: At times, vehicles have to stop to allow these residents to pass safely.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: The Town Council and HDB could not even cut the shrubs and lay some concrete slab to create a simple footpath at the fringe of the private estate for residents to walk safely as the turf is now sitting on private land as well.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: The Town Council has to repatch the power supply from one of the nearest HDB blocks in the estate or else residents, especially school students, will have to walk in the dark every morning to the bus stop at Hougang Avenue 7.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: And who is responsible to maintain the HDB car park service road now that it is made to serve both public and private estates after privatisation?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: Were there any considerations given to replace footpaths for residents due to safety concerns?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: I urge the Ministry to look into this and address the safety issues as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Aljunied-Hougang Town Council (AHTC) has also been receiving similar feedback from residents living in other parts of the town.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Town Council has conducted checks on the in-car fan system for these respective lifts and found that everything is good and running well.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: After much observation, it was suspected that the metal lift shaft might be the main contributing factor.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I am quite confident this could be the reason because, for Kaki Bukit ward, the affected residents who feedback on this issue stay in blocks where the lift shafts are exposed to the direct afternoon sun.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: During my recent house visit to one of the affected blocks, a resident expressed concern over this matter.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: He cited an example of a man trapped in such a situation during a hot day.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The trapped passenger, especially one who is an elderly or an individual who has medical conditions, may experience related complications, such as dehydration, respiratory problems and, in the worst-case scenario, a heat stroke, due to the condition of the lift.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Chairman, trees and greenery are an unmistakable part of the Singapore story since Independence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: However, removing a tree is probably one of the hardest things to do for any Town Council.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My understanding is that HDB and NParks officers tend to err on the side of caution and would prefer to leave a tree in its place and take the position that a mature tree should not be cut down if that outcome can be avoided; and I can understand this position.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: However, exceptions should be made in selected cases and one occasion is during the HDB's periodic cyclical HDB car park upgrading exercises.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: A few years ago, the surface area at Block 601 Bedok Reservoir Road was upgraded by the HDB, upgrading that comes by once every 25-odd years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Chopping off a part of the route by the Town Council contractors to reinstate the car park slabs and prevent slabs from popping up pose a high risk of destabilising the tree.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: As this problem is more unique to mature HDB estates, a parallel concern is the increasing number of elderly who misjudge the height of curbs damaged by overgrown trees.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This problem should be addressed with a holistic assessment that is not encumbered by conservation concerns alone but takes safety considerations and the long-term maintenance costs to the Town Council in mind as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The current HDB requirement to plant three new trees for every one fell would ensure that Singapore remains a city full of trees and greenery.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand from NParks' Tree Management Programme published in January 2013 that tree inspection details are recorded and entered into a database.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For how long are these records required to be kept in the database?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The process should be a fact-finding exercise, and evidence such as the manner in which the inspections were conducted and what was looked for during those inspections should be preserved to ensure the integrity of the fact-finding process during investigations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In cases of injury or death, a rigorous investigation into the facts of the case conducted by an independent third party may also better assist affected families to seek closure.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The names we put on public buildings become part of our nation's consciousness, a collective memory for present and future generations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Had there not been a public outcry over naming rights, the sports hub and facilities flanking our National Stadium might be known as OCBC World today.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our public universities, too, are dotted with many examples, like the College of Alice and Peter Tan, and the Mochtar Riady Building.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the generosity of donors should be encouraged and accorded due appreciation, what kind of message are we sending by naming even a children's playground after a corporate entity?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Apart from sports, what about the naming of other landmark facilities, such as our public hospitals?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Understandably, naming these hospitals after the two donors has caused controversy, with public chatter that the naming rights were sold relatively cheaply.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could and should the hospitals have been named in a more meaningful way?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What safeguards are there against donors who may be trying to shore up their reputation in the name of philanthropy?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The issue is even trickier when the donor is a living person, as his legacy could always turn from good to bad if he gets into personal, financial or legal problems later.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The question is to what extent the names of our public buildings should be sold to the highest bidder.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Should we have loftier aspirations instead, by naming public facilities to reflect ideals rather than wealth?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In comparison, names like the Lim Bo Seng Memorial bring abundantly more to the national consciousness and to future generations.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What measures have been implemented to prevent their reoccurrence and assist these farms?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What have been the long- and short-term impact on our coastal seawater, beaches and marine life due to these spills?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What measures can we take to mitigate the impact of global warming on our marine life?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Indeed, despite having many built-up areas, we also have pockets of greenery, such as our many parks and nature reserves that provide a respite from the hustle and bustle of urban living.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: What is also significant is the amount of greenery that has been incorporated into our buildings and built structures.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: This is something that MNDs' two agencies, URA and NParks, have worked hard to achieve, and has also rooted the strength and success of our landscape architecture industry.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: In high-rise and urban greenery, landscaping must not be seen as a form of "green-washing" or an afterthought.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: As space becomes scarcer in Singapore and our living areas become denser, it is all the more important to ensure that proper landscaping and carefully integrated and designed greenery help to enhance not just the aesthetics of the development, but the holistic mental and emotional wellness of the individuals working and living in that development as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: This would be in line with the CFE's strategy to "plan boldly for growth and city rejuvenation".

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: I would thus like to encourage MND to work with landscape architecture companies and bodies, such as the Singapore Institute of Landscape Architects (SILA), to develop and enhance the industry in terms of talent development, opening up pathways for career growth and also raising the professional standing of landscape architects.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: This growth could not only be in terms of enhancing the domestic landscape industry, but perhaps we could also use our expertise and leverage on our "City-in-a Garden" reputation to support our landscape architects to make an impact regionally and internationally as well.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Chairman, the plan to develop the Rail Corridor is a welcome one.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Several groups of Singaporeans are looking forward to the potential upside the 24-kilometre (km) master plan will bring, from nature and recreation to tourism and history.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For nature lovers, it is a much-awaited oasis and urban respite and a chance to learn about Singapore's biodiversity.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In terms of recreation, the Rail Corridor will offer attractive choices − cycling paths, running tracks, rock-climbing, cafes and even an outdoor cinema.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For history lovers, the Rail Corridor will restore to the area its historical significance and promote greater appreciation of the Singapore-Malaya rail link that started in 1903.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Also in the vicinity is the gallery: "Surviving the Japanese Occupation: War and its Legacies".

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The confluence of rich history, greenery and recreational opportunities in the Rail Corridor makes it a unique experience and attraction that can enhance tourism.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The Rail Corridor could very well become Singapore's iconic equivalent to New York City's High Line, which is an old railway transformed into one of the most innovative and inviting green public spaces in Manhattan.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The High Line is now a favourite spot for New Yorkers and tourists alike.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To reap the same success as the High Line, access and transport to the area is vital.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Residents in Hume, who live in the backyard of the Rail Corridor, are keen to know the status of developments of this upcoming iconic attraction.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For instance, will the anticipated rise in human traffic to the area be a key factor for the building of an MRT station in Hume?

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Or do the authorities foresee the potential traffic to the Rail Corridor and its attractiveness, and so act in tandem to boost Singaporeans' enjoyment of our rich heritage and also enhance the tourist experience with good and easy access to the Corridor?

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Does MND regard the site as having potential for further developments?

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The potential movement of people to the Rail Corridor is immense.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Trade and Industry and the Ministers for Education (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With its unique proposition as a residential and community oasis as well as promising tourist spot, we hope MND will give serious consideration to the surrounding developments of the Rail Corridor so as to enhance the area's liveability and attractiveness, making Singapore an endearing home and also a distinctive global city.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am glad the media picked up the topic and did an excellent documentary on the Sembawang hot spring, which attracted a lot of public attention.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The Sembawang hot spring has a lot of potential as a recreational and educational spot.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I share the sentiments of many Sembawang residents and fellow MPs that the place should not be too commercialised and, as far as possible, to maintain the rustic kampong atmosphere.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As the Prime Minister mentioned, old models are not working, new models are coming in thick and fast and we are having to adjust and keep up because of technology and globalisation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: And the disruption will happen over and over again, relentlessly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: For example, a person is allowed to rent out the property for 50 nights a year for a start.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: If there are legitimate complaints received, then the licence can be revoked or the number of nights decreased.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: A review can be made each year and, if URA is satisfied, the number of nights can be increased or, if they are not satisfied, they can be decreased.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The property owner is thus incentivised to ensure that no disamenities are caused.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In this case, the ball is in the court of the guests to ensure that no disamenities were caused to avoid forfeiting the deposit.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I urge the Ministry to consider this proposal and ensure that we embrace and regulate rather than ban this disruptive innovation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, they were paying off the loan on the flat, without the benefit of rental income, and being overseas working and paying for their own upkeep overseas as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Would MND and HDB be able to look into how we can better support our young Singaporeans, as we regionalise our economy?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: He told me that he had a season parking lot for his lorry along Yishun Avenue 1.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: However, some parking lots had been removed recently and by the time he came back late at night, there were no parking lots available.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Hence, when he continues to park along Yishun Avenue 1, he received summonses from LTA.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: They told me that they will do a quick check.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: About a month later, on 16 January 2017, another resident came to see me, telling me the same problem.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Is he expected to remember which area to light-touch and which area not to light-touch?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Some of my poor residents had paid up the fines.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: They came to see only when they − if I may put it in their language − "buay tahan liao, diam diam dio".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: The last time I heard, it was six months to a year, now is it better?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Mr Desmond Lee)
text: Mr Chairman, in the course of my presentation, may I have your permission to show some slides and a video?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: People have to travel out of the city to connect with nature.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As a city-state, we have taken quite a different approach from Day 1.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our nature reserves and the nature parks that buffer them are green gems in the heart of the city.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Biodiversity hotspots are connected through urban areas by nature parks, nature ways and lush streetscape greenery.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Nature envelops our urban city completely, as greenery courses through the veins of our cityscape and now, up our skyline.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Being in such close proximity to nature, there is so much that Wild Singapore offers us.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As Ms Ria Tan, a nature advocate, often says, and I quote: "Singapore is probably the only place in the world where one can visit a rainforest, a mangrove and a coral reef, all within half an hour from our city".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Proximity to nature, however, means increased human-wildlife interactions and the potential for conflicts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Today, Singapore is recognised by experts and academics as a Biophilic City, where nature and greenery are integral to our design and planning.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As the Minister said earlier, we have the opportunity to take things to the next level where people learn to co-exist more harmoniously with our natural heritage and wildlife.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This can only be achieved through extensive outreach and education and by different stakeholders working together as stewards of our natural heritage and adopting a scientific approach to managing urban ecologies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: MND will work closely with our nature groups and animal welfare groups, as well as our Friends of the Park communities, and find opportunities in the course of the year to share more of our thoughts with fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Many stakeholders have played a part in greening our city.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I join Mr Darryl David in affirming the efforts of our landscape architecture industry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NParks collaborates with the Singapore Institute of Landscape Architects (SILA) to establish industry best practices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It supports SILA's accreditation programme through workshops and seminars in horticulture and landscaping, for continuous professional development.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NParks also partners SILA and the Landscape Industry Association of Singapore (LIAS) to organise international trade shows and conferences and promote knowledge-sharing and showcase industry development.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Ms Low Yen Ling asked about the Rail Corridor.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This stretch is rich in greenery and heritage.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will invite public feedback to help us assess their suitability for the Corridor.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When this four-km stretch is completed, residents can look forward to a trail that people of all ages and abilities can use, and basic amenities, such as toilets, drinking fountains and bicycle rentals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak asked about the Sembawang hot spring.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NParks will continue to gather more feedback from the community and residents on design.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui asked about the impact of oil spills, algae blooms and global warming on our marine biodiversity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Studies show that this is the best way to help our ecosystems withstand and recover from the impact of climate change, including algal blooms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our Pioneers in the built environment sector have built up our world-class infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We need to look at new ways to construct our future City.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We want our built environment sector to be technologically-advanced, coordinated across the entire construction value chain, and be supported by a highly-skilled workforce with a strong Singaporean Core of professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This means bringing in contractors at the design stage so that the model will be close to what will eventually be built.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The digital model will then be sent to a one-stop portal for coordinated regulatory approvals, and rules-based automated checking can speed this up.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For those who are not familiar, early contractor involvement is a kind of procurement method where contractors are engaged early, in fact, right upfront, to provide inputs into the design of a project.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For traditional procurement, contractors will bid for a project based on a fixed design and they cannot influence the design upfront.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In contrast, early contractor involvement (ECI) allows the input of contractors to be incorporated at the design stage.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As I have said, this reduces abortive work and leads to potential time and cost savings for the project.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, contractors do need to commit more resources for ECI, as they are expected to develop detailed design solutions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That said, the BCA's guide on ECI limits the number of tenderers under ECI to a maximum of five.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This seeks to strike a balance between giving good tender options to ensure value for money and good design, while increasing the opportunities of winning the bids for tenderers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In addition, tenderers are compensated for their efforts to come up with concept designs submitted for the ECI tender even if they are unsuccessful.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, as part of an effort to bring design in a detailed fashion upstream, we have to strike a balance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The approved plans will be sent to suppliers in highly automated Integrated Construction and Pre-fabrication Hubs (ICPHs).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Once completed, Design for Manufacturing and Assembly (DfMA) components will be sent, just in time, to be assembled onsite.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Now I will just ask Members to watch a very short video which will show what DfMA is all about and what we are aspiring to achieve.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, this is a video of an ICPH where robotics and machinery set moulds and concrete is cast, again using machinery, with precision quality control of each component.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The prefabricated members are then packed once they are completed and are then sent by logistics to site, just in time to be assembled at the worksite.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But getting there is challenging, especially in times of economic uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But private sector demand is expected to remain subdued.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Earlier, Er Dr Lee and Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked how we can help construction firms during this period.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Government will push out a strong pipeline of major infrastructure projects in the next few years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And to put things in perspective, in 2012, five years ago, the public sector demand accounted for about 30% of overall construction demand, with the private sector taking up 70%.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And in 2017 and over the next few years, we might expect this ratio to flip around, with the public sector accounting for about 70% of overall demand.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These will be smaller projects, like upgrading of Community Clubs (CCs), sports facilities and Neighbourhood Police Posts and Centres (NPCs), which our small and medium enterprises (SMEs) can bid for.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will also encourage public agencies to parcel out larger projects into smaller ones, where appropriate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will help diversify risk and enable more local firms to participate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In the long run, the best thing we can do is to help our local companies remain competitive by strengthening their capabilities and improving their productivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our Construction Productivity and Capability Fund (CPCF) subsidises this process to help our firms level up.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will monitor if more measures are needed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This period of uncertainty is a reminder that we need to strengthen our Built Environment sector by becoming more productive and future-ready.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is why we have been partnering the industry at every step of the way, especially when it comes to improving productivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our efforts since the first Construction Productivity Roadmap in 2010 have yielded results.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Almost $800 million has been made available to firms through CPCF.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: One local contractor, as an example, Teambuild Engineering and Construction tapped on CPCF funding to develop a new prototype for concrete PPVC that can be better used for high-rise buildings and they are piloting this prototype at a residential project.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This new system can potentially improve productivity by up to 40%.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we will continue to assist firms through various funding schemes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But these funds are for them to apply and seize in order to innovate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In tandem, our workers are becoming more skilled.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Nearly 40% of construction workers are now at the higher-skilled (R1) level.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It was only 20% in 2014 and just 2% in 2011.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To sustain this momentum, BCA will consult the industry to review the minimum R1 requirements at firm level.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I encourage firms to tap on Government subsidised funding schemes to upgrade their workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our annual site productivity, which measures work done per man-day, has also improved by 2% per year from 2014 to 2016.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Compare this to a mere 0.3% per year in 2010.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we aim to achieve 2.5% to 4% annual site productivity improvements from now till 2020.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To achieve our productivity targets, we encourage the industry to adopt prefabrication technologies along the DfMA continuum.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Offsite construction requires less labour onsite and shortens project time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As Er Dr Lee Bee Wah pointed out, DfMA is not just about PPVC.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is a broad spectrum to choose from, including as you can see from the slide, Mass Engineered Timber (MET), advanced precast structural steel and other DfMA technologies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are looking to pilot a GLS site that will specify construction productivity outcomes without mandating specific technologies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will give firms the flexibility to propose suitable technologies to meet the productivity outcomes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To help increase our supply resilience for DfMA technologies, we will provide incentives to help more firms set up DfMA manufacturing facilities locally.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will extend the Land Intensification Allowance (LIA) scheme to cover the construction of ICPHs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: ICPHs are high-density and highly-automated factories that manufacture DfMA components shown in the short video earlier.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Currently, we have four sites for ICPHs and will be launching more in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The scheme will provide tax relief on the capital investment needed to develop ICPHs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will share more details of this later.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To help lower this premium, the public sector will continue to take the lead to generate demand.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will allow us to roll out more tenders to benefit progressive builders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, some of MOE's upcoming sports halls will include the use of MET, and some of JTC's industrial premises will use structural steel.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have consulted extensively and will continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While still a work-in-progress, some preliminary ideas are to further adopt DfMA technology, do more digital engineering and encourage firms to internationalise to have access to new markets.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Government will take the lead in adopting digital technology in the Built environment sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We need to act swiftly to harness these benefits or we will be left behind.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, recently, I met some executives from a built environment firm which have ventured overseas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They said that they benefited from the regulatory requirement to use BIM in Singapore, and felt that it would be a competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But when they went to these overseas markets, firms from that market were already using digital technologies, BIM, even though the regulators in that country were not BIM-enabled, had no rules mandating it, did not know what to do with the BIM models.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, the foreign firms had to dumb down their 3D models into 2D designs to submit as regulatory submissions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Yet, these firms overseas, without compulsion, saw the competitive edge that BIM and digital technology offered them in their own market and around the world.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That is why our ITM has initiatives to increase the adoption of BIM and Virtual Design and Construction (VDC).

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is a virtual design and construction project, MapleTree Business City 2.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, if you have visited the BCA virtual laboratory and put on 3D goggles like what the firms do, you will literally be able to walk through the entire building, room to room, and be able to build virtually first, and then build onsite in reality.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This helps prevent abortive work downstream as architects, engineers and contractors can identify and fix problems before construction starts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are also improving implementation on the ground.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We hear Er Dr Lee Bee Wah that BIM models are sometimes less useful because they lack the information required for construction planning.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, the architects put up one set to meet regulatory requirements, but they do not have enough information in the BIM model and, as a result, the contractors have had to redo everything, because they have to look at it from a construction angle.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: BCA is working with the industry to bridge this gap by developing a Code of Practice.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This Code of Practice will set out what the architects and engineers need to include in the model to make it more useful in a collaborative fashion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To help our firms take up BIM and VDC, we will continue to provide funding support for collaborative BIM projects.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We encourage firms to apply for these generous schemes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We need to build up industry capabilities in BIM and VDC and we encourage our firms to send their employees to attend BIM and VDC training at the BCA Academy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: New features will include rules-based automated checking software.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will improve service delivery and achieve higher productivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I met Ms Eunice Chen at BCA's Young Leaders Retreat in November last year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: She started off as an architect, recently upgraded herself by pursuing a Master of Science in Real Estate in the National University of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Currently, as a Project Manager in Far East Organization, she is working with a team of consultants using BIM for a commercial project in Woodlands.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Information technology, digital technology like BIM and VDC opens up exciting and better opportunities for our millennials.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, I meet from time to time the young leaders of the built environment sector − the young architects, engineers and quantity surveyors - and they share with me how they look forward to this transformation and how technology can be used to bring our future city to a different level.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For these young millennials, they take to technology like fish to water.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In a sense, this process will take time and move with the generations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In the long run, growing our built environment sector means looking beyond our shores.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As Er Dr Lee Bee Wah said, there is a limit to what we can build here.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But as the region develops, there will be increasing demand for sophisticated infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To venture overseas, companies need scale and niche competencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Government will help the industry achieve these aims as much as we can.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, during one of our subcommittee meetings, one member of the built environment sector, an industry player, asked, "Well, how big a fish can you grow in Singapore?" Certainly, we can be nimble, sophisticated and productive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While we cannot be a big fish competing overseas, we could perhaps go as a school of fish, integrating across different sectors, different members of the value chain, going overseas under the Singapore brand, competing effectively.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will update this House on the results of the internationalisation taskforce's work when ready.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Taken together, these moves bring us closer to realising our vision of a productive and progressive sector that provides good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For existing estates, we also need to constantly rejuvenate them so that they remain vibrant and liveable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: First, at the town level, the Remaking Our Heartland 3 (ROH3) programme adopts a ground-up consultative approach to conceptualise the rejuvenation of existing towns.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, for instance, in Woodlands, there will be a new "Community Nexus" located at the Admiralty MRT station that will serve as a "one-stop" hub of amenities for the residents, comprising new and existing facilities, such as Kampung Admiralty, the Admiralty Place Neighbourhood Centre and the Woodlands Galaxy Community Club.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In Pasir Ris, residents can look forward to an enhanced walking and cycling experience with more facilities and greenery along key connections in the town.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In Toa Payoh, the familiar "Ring Road", formed by Lorong 1 and Lorong 6 Toa Payoh will be enlivened with cycling paths to link facilities and transport nodes and pocket parks to provide rest points and gathering spaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will soon be holding public exhibitions in April and May this year where everyone can view the initial plans and provide another round of feedback.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, at the neighbourhood level, the Neighbourhood Renewal Programme (NRP) will continue to facilitate estate rejuvenation, focusing on precinct and block level improvements.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also enhanced the Revitalisation of Shops (ROS) Scheme last year to help neighbourhood shops in the HDB heartlands to rejuvenate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Responses from HDB shop keepers and the Merchants' Associations have been positive: the number of applications for ROS upgrading works last year was the highest we have seen since the scheme was introduced in 2007.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: By the end of the programme, more than 300,000 flats built up to 1986 will benefit.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So far, we have spoken about the building of our future city, the design of new estates and the rejuvenation of existing towns.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: An equally important but less frequently talked about aspect of our work is the active maintenance of our city, estates and infrastructure as they age.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Maintainability should be an important consideration in building design.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: HDB, for example, takes into account maintenance considerations upfront in the design of BTO and upgrading projects, with a focus on design and detailing, materials and finishes and access for maintainability.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As our infrastructure ages, we will need to spend more on maintenance and replacement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Often, we focus on building and building more but do not recognise enough the very long tail of maintenance, replacement and repair.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A good example is the maintenance of lifts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As with all machinery, lifts need to be maintained regularly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They have a limited lifespan before they need to be replaced.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Lift owners, Town Councils and the lift maintenance industry all have a part to play in keeping our lifts reliable and safe.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have taken active steps on two fronts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Second, we have enhanced BCA's regulatory regime to strengthen our oversight of lifts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Third, we are also working with the industry to ensure a competent and sustainable lift maintenance workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These include building up technical competencies, attracting more locals to the sector, and improving productivity by encouraging the adoption of new technologies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On a related note, Mr Faisal Manap suggested that better heat insulation for lift shafts that are exposed to direct sunlight be provided.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I do not have exact details but we will follow up on that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Generally, to mitigate the heat built up in lift shafts, an insulation layer is incorporated in the cladding for all lifts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The lift cars are also designed to be well-ventilated with mechanical fans to improve the air quality and to purge trapped heat when the car doors open.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For lift shafts that are exposed to direct sunlight, additional measures, such as increasing the capacity of the mechanical fans or programming the lift cars to allow the lift doors to remain open when not in use, can be adopted.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But I do not know the details of Mr Faisal Manap's case; we will follow up on it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Another aspect of maintenance we have been looking at is our building facades all over the city.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Presently, BCA requires building owners to ensure that their buildings, including exterior features like windows and air-conditioning units, are properly maintained.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: BCA can require rectification if maintenance is poor.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For HDB blocks, while maintenance of facades comes under the purview of the Town Councils, HDB has in place several measures to assist them, such as the co-payment scheme, since 2004 for the repair of facade finishes, audit inspection checks by HDB officers and conducting technical training for all Town Councils twice a year since 2010.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Through normal wear and tear, older facades will need added maintenance and we are looking into enhancing the regulatory framework on facades, for both public and private buildings, to ensure that facades and exterior features are well-maintained, regularly inspected and remain properly secured.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is important for us, as a City-in-a-Garden, with some seven million trees around the island.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we are deeply saddened each time such incidents cause injury or loss of life.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Behind the scenes, NParks officers and contractors work hard to ensure that trees are healthy and safe.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NParks has a comprehensive tree management programme that includes a regime of inspections and pruning.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Tree inspection is carried out only by certified professionals and records are digitalised to facilitate information retrieval and to ensure that trees under NParks are checked and maintained according to schedule.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This system also enables NParks to zoom in on and pre-emptively replace storm-vulnerable trees.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For fatal incidents, NParks will assist the Police Investigation Officer (IO) in his/her investigation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Independent arborists may also be engaged by NParks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Given the more unpredictable weather conditions, NParks has stepped up inspections and taken measures to improve the general health of our trees.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These include routine mulching to supplement the application of fertilisers, and pruning techniques to improve tree structure and balance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NParks is also developing modelling techniques to better understand the structural behaviour of trees under heavy rain and wind and also in micro-climatic conditions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Pritam Singh has suggested that we review tree replacement guidelines in mature HDB estates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He has articulated various examples that his Town Council had encountered.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When trees need to be removed, HDB seeks to ensure that existing levels of greenery are generally maintained.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Hence, his reference to the tree replacement ratios.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These tree replacement guidelines, therefore, take into consideration the size and amount of shade provided by the affected tree.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: HDB works closely with NParks to identify appropriate tree species for residential estates and takes into account existing site conditions, such as valuable planting space and proximity to residential blocks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: NParks and HDB are also mindful that when you plant trees in estates, you also need to take care of its impact on residents, such as falling leaves, branches, insects, birds and tree roots.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Town Councils can also propose alternative replacement tree species for HDB to consider.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In general, the tree species should suit the existing landscape and site conditions, take into account residents' considerations and provide sufficient shade and are easy to maintain.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At times, tree removal is necessary if a tree poses a risk to public safety or where trees are affected by new developments, upgrading or construction works.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: HDB's approval is required for all tree removal requests in HDB estates except where it is assessed that the tree may fall at any moment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In such cases, Town Councils should remove the tree first without HDB's prior approval and report the matter to HDB.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These guidelines have served HDB well thus far, but we will bear the Member's concerns in mind.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked for more heavy vehicle parking in Yishun.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The issue is not at the national level; the issue is at the local level, as the Member is well aware.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is not possible to fully meet demand for overnight parking of heavy vehicles through public heavy vehicle parks that are in or near residential areas as this is likely to pose a nuisance and traffic hazard to residents, especially the elderly and the young.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Instead, we are ramping up the number of heavy vehicle parking lots within private industrial developments, and do so whenever we launch such sites, including those in the northern part of Singapore, such as Yishun.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In addition, heavy vehicle owners should provide transport arrangements for their drivers if they cannot help them find a lot near their drivers' homes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And we are actively looking at measures to achieve this.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Louis Ng has suggested various ways to facilitate short-term rentals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: His point is: do not kill innovation, embrace it, go with the flow.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But on our part, we also have to balance various interests − those who wish to ride on the new economy, the sharing economy and also those who have a right to enjoy peace and quiet in their home environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng spoke about flexibility in the implementation of the Minimum Occupancy Period (MOP) to support young Singaporeans taking on overseas postings.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As HDB flats are meant for owner occupation, flat owners have to fulfil an MOP before they can sublet their whole flat.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Png Eng Huat raised some concerns about the impact of privatisation of HUDC estates in Hougang.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I do not have all the details of each of these concerns he and his residents face.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But I understand that, for Hougang Avenue 7, and this is based on what available information I have, I understand that the Member has raised this specific issue to HDB.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: HDB is currently looking into options to construct a footpath for the residents, where feasible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If the Member has further questions or issues to raise, please surface them to us.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, imagine if there is a grass field that becomes a GLS site and there is a pathway that people normally use to get quickly to, say, the market or the MRT station, during the GLS site launch, where feasible, we will put that easement or right of way in some form as a condition.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On Ms Sylvia Lim's query on how public building names are approved, and to what extent donors can insist on naming rights, I would like to share that the Street and Building Names Board (SBNB) oversees the approval of names of buildings, estates and streets in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For a select group of public buildings, such as education institutions under MOE, military installations under MINDEF, and community sports facilities under Sport Singapore, the relevant Government agencies need not seek the Board's approval for the naming and they will have their policies on the naming of such institutions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In general, in approving building names, the agencies ensure that the proposed names are appropriate in the context of what the building is, where it is located and what it is used for.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In addition, the selected name should seek to reflect the character of the place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The societal, historical and cultural context of the surroundings are also important considerations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some public buildings may be named after organisations or foundations to recognise significant philanthropic or other contributions to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Generally, when assessing the suitability of a name, the relevant Government agencies will assess the credibility and reputation of the proposed name and check to ensure that it does not undermine the associated interests and larger identity of the named public building.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In transforming our built environment sector, the Government will continue to take the lead and assist our businesses in making the transition.
