speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In rejuvenating our estates, we are taking active steps to involve the community and we will continue to step up our maintenance efforts and regulatory regimes to enhance the living environment for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: With these efforts, we look forward to an even more exciting living environment, as well as a bright future for Singaporeans of all ages and abilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Today, I would like to draw attention to the closely related issue of food security.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: There are many similarities here with the water security issue.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Like water, agricultural and food products are an essential resource, for which it is imperative that we find stable sources of supply.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: As in the case of water, the fact that our supermarket shelves are constantly stocked may have dulled us to the reality of our intrinsic vulnerability on this front.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Across the world, the issue of managing food and agricultural resources will only grow in importance.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: This is because the world's population is growing, living standards are improving and households in developing countries are moving up the income ladder.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: The demand for food products that are typically consumed by households in that income strata will only increase − milk, cheese, meat and fish.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Furthermore, the threat of climate change has also added a new dimension to uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Extreme weather events can cause disruptions in agricultural output, lead to spikes and volatility in prices of key agricultural commodities.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Over the past few years, we have seen on occasions news reports of mass fish deaths in our Singapore waters and kelongs, which our marine biologists have described as an indirect consequence of warmer temperatures that cause marine plankton to swell and compete for oxygen with our local fish population.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: These instances are important reminders of our unique vulnerabilities on this front.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Where possible, what efforts are ongoing to boost the local sources of agricultural and food products?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Is there a clear roadmap ahead to develop our local farming supply?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: How does the Government plan to overcome the inherent land constraints that we face?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: And on the external front, are we actively seeking to diversify our sources of food imports in order to improve the resilience of our overall food supply chains?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Realistically, while it is likely that we will always have to end up importing the majority of the food that we consume, it is nevertheless heartening to know that there have been attempts to leverage technology and innovation to promote agriculture and aquaculture in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: As the global population continues to grow, there might be uncertainty whether global food supply can keep up with demand, especially in these uncertain times when countries are becoming more and more inward-looking.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Also, while technology might be needed to enhance farming, aquaculture and the rearing of livestock in terms of techniques, the product does increasingly end up being enhanced as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: While this is acceptable to a certain degree, we also do not want to end up with food that have been genetically modified too much or enhanced too much as we would then be concerned about the potential negative effects of such food.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Would MND be able to give more information on how the Government intends to ensure that our food supply will remain safe and secure?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong, you have three cuts.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: During last year's COS debate, the Ministry declared that strengthening our food security will be a priority in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Whilst the world faces a period of global food supply uncertainty, as the UN Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) warned in a report last month, due to a growing global population, global agricultural output will need to increase by 50%.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This means that we are highly vulnerable when food crises occur.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given the scarcity of resources, self-sufficiency does not necessarily just refer to increasing production.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Reducing wastage will help us to do more with less.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is, therefore, important to look at or tackle food wastage.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides conducting ongoing public education to urge Singaporeans not to waste food, we should also encourage retailers and food sellers to provide the option of smaller portions for sale so that consumers will not have to throw away food they cannot finish.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the US, under the Good Samaritan Act, companies are not liable for anything that happens to those who consume the food they donated.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are we able to adopt similar legislation to encourage more companies to step forward and donate unsold food that is still suitable for consumption?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In recent years, our 117 coastal fish farms have had to deal with an increasing number of oil spills and occurrences of harmful algae blooms.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What measures does the Ministry have to prevent their recurrence and manage longer-term environmental risks?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have another six fish farms on land.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will the Ministry assist more fish farms to convert to indoor, vertical farms for better control of the environmental factors?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Apollo Aquaculture Group will be setting up a high-tech farm in Brunei.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there plans to set up similar farms nearer to Singapore?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In 2011, we began a push to increase the percentage of fish from our farms to 15% of the fish eaten here.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When will we be able to achieve our initial target?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Twenty-five percent of our eggs come from three local egg farms.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the target for the next five years?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How much of the chicken meat consumed here are locally farmed?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Do we have plans to increase production from local farms?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Have there been studies done on overseas contract farming?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is our long-term target for vegetables and fruits grown locally?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister share what innovative technologies are being used to improve quality, productivity and output for our agriculture sector?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To date, how much of the funds have been utilised?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the progress of our acquisition of farmland overseas by the Government and Singaporean companies and our partnerships with foreign agricultural companies?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are estates that are built in the 1960s and 1970s and are still not selected for the Estate Upgrading Programme (EUP).

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Soo Chow Garden, Adelphi Park and Pemimpin estates date back to the 1960s and 1970s, and there are portions which have fallen into disrepair.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In dire need of attention are the unduly narrow footpaths and pavements.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Those in wheelchairs and babies in prams have to be pushed on the roads.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With cars parked by the side, the roads are, in fact, congested and highly dangerous to both the road users and pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some parts of the playgrounds and parks are also in bad shape.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Community bonding has been affected as a result, since the parks are usual gathering points for the residents.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need the EUP to prevent the shared public areas from deteriorating into safety and health hazards.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If EUP cannot be sped up, as my appeal to the Ministry last year showed, would it be possible for a special fund to be set up for urgent repairs, maintenance and upgrading works at private estates, where factors, such as safety and health, are of immediate concern?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Minister also consider the number of residents living in the estate as one of the criteria during the selection process?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If the estate has a higher density of residents, it makes sense to give it priority, other things being equal, as more people stand to benefit from the upgrading.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My third cut is on real estate and real estate-related industries.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I declare my interest as a professional in the real estate industry.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In land-scarce Singapore, how do we foster more innovations in real estate development, so as to meet the needs of consumers and cultivate a sustainable market for real estate developers and real estate-related businesses, whilst achieving optimum land use efficiency?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Last November, the Minister mentioned that the Government is considering new partnership models with the private sector.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One is the "master developer" approach where developers can do the master planning and optimise different land uses in an integrated manner for large parcels of land.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For developers in overseas markets, they have the opportunities to develop: (a) a township; (b) they could build entertainment complexes, such as a golf course and theme park, to enhance the surrounding residential or commercial development; or (c) they could build schools and hospitals or other public facilities which would be handed over to the relevant authorities to operate, with rights to develop real estate for residential or commercial use.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In these instances, the developer has the flexibility to plan and execute the development in phases and adopt varied sales and marketing strategies to achieve its return objectives, while complying with the tender specifications by the authorities.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would this be a possibility in Singapore, given the land constraints?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Perhaps the development of certain Southern Islands can adopt such an approach.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Property owners and retailers work together to decide on how to create and build an attractive BID.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Minister please elaborate on these schemes?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These collaborative approaches have had good results when implemented in other countries and I look forward to the Minister's updates about their feasibility in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we are a densely populated and highly built-up city, such measures will have a great impact.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Will AVA consider taking similar steps to improve transparency in our food labels?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Next, the Love Cats pilot programme, managed by the Cat Welfare Society and conducted in Chong Pang between 2012 and 2016, achieved far-reaching effects to help the Town Council, AVA and relevant agencies better tackle cat-related disputes in the community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In support of this pilot, MND provided a two-year grant.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: However, funding has since stopped, though the pilot continued with a robust mediation and resident engagement model, with much success in resolving neighbourly issues related to cats.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Will the Ministry consider supporting and extending the funding of this pilot to more estates in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: To strengthen enforcement at our checkpoints, several non-government organisations (NGOs) have suggested the establishment of a sniffer dog programme, used effectively by many countries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Sniffer dogs are highly efficient at detecting contraband and also serve a deterrent function.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In South Korea, a dog named Simba detected major finds almost every month, totaling 142 separate animal parts and some "live" animals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In Hong Kong, sniffer dogs can detect ivory concealed in packages in just under five seconds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: From 2008 to 2015, the dogs assisted in over 40 cases of smuggled animals or products and can identify 15 endangered species.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: AVA stated that the sniffer dog programme was "less cost-effective than other measures".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can AVA clarify what the other measures are and whether they are already in place?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: While other AVA, ICA and customs officers assist in detecting wildlife crime, it is clearly insufficient to have only three inspectors solely dedicated towards tackling wildlife crime in Singapore, considering as well that this is a 24/7 job.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can the Ministry increase resources and manpower for this section, considering again that Singapore continues to remain in the spotlight with regard to wildlife crime.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: However, AVA continues to face substantial challenges in investigations, including the lack of eyewitnesses and direct evidence, as well as an increase in online crimes.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We are, to some extent, "vulnerable" in our food supply because we lack natural resources to grow all the food that we will ever need.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But we have never passively accepted our fate as it is.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Just look at how we deal with our water issue.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It is an existential vulnerability, but we have gradually strengthened our water supply through our "Four National Taps".

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our water story has been about transforming adversity into opportunity.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I believe we can do the same with food by embracing technology.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We can intensify land use, as some Members have suggested, reduce wastage and increase the yields of our farms.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We can transform our small but vibrant farm sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And as some Members have noted, with global population growth and more extreme weather patterns, it is time for us to think ahead.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The first of these baskets is imports from around the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is key because we do not have enough land to cultivate all that we need.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But diversification makes this basket much more resilient.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, we will continue our efforts to look for more varied sources of food for import.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This opens up new markets and helps our farms overcome land constraints in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We want to help local farms and food companies venture abroad to seek opportunities.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Brunei is keen to attract our farmers as a way of diversifying their economy and, for us, we are interested to find alternative sources of food supply and for cultivation of the food that we need as well.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We had good bilateral discussions among ourselves, the delegation and the Bruneian officials.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We also want some value-added operations to remain in Singapore, things like research and development (R&D), training, development of technology and innovation.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In fact, some of our Singapore agriculture specialists have actually done so.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That number alone would approximate the annual total output from all the fish farms in Singapore, just from this one farm.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Another local farm, Sky Greens, has ventured to Hainan in China.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I shared about the development of Sky Greens at the COS last year and this year, I am happy to show that Sky Greens has taken a step further by also internationalising into China.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They have deployed their vertical farming towers on 0.23 hectares in Hainan Island in China, and they plan to develop 20 hectares more.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Members have asked if local farms continue to play an important role.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I say this is an important part of our food security because it provides a critical buffer against global supply shocks for especially key food items like vegetables, food fish and eggs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It cannot be business as usual if our local production is needed to strengthen our food resilience.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, the targets that we set are reviewed from time to time as our needs evolve and as technology becomes available.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Realistically, though, Singapore is too small to develop large tracts of land for farming.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will never have enough land to ever grow all the food that we need.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Just as we ask our SMEs in various other sectors to transform, automate, be more productive and to take on automation, we need our agricultural players to transform into one that is more productive as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We need to adopt modern practices and embrace technology as a multiplier to do more with less.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We have been working with our farmers to help them raise their production levels.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Over the past year, we have increased engagement with our local farms because they know the issues and challenges best as practitioners on the ground.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We have visited them over the last six to nine months, spoken with them, seen how they operate and understand some of the constraints that they have and what they see as opportunities for the farming sector.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To enable our local farmers to play an active role in transforming our farming sector, we formed an Industry Consultation Panel (ICP) early this year.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It consists of progressive farmers representing various food farm types, as well as academics who can help translate research in agricultural technology into practical implementation in our farms.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Together, practitioners, academics and policymakers will work together to innovate, co-create and transform our farming sector through technology.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Many Singaporeans and, in fact, Members have asked whether local farming has a future in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That is a fundamental question, and I would say the answer is an unequivocal yes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Farming will be a part of Singapore's future.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But it will have to be a different-looking farming sector from what it is today in order for the sector to fulfil its important role of strengthening Singapore's food supply resilience and food security.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I have already spoken about Sky Greens and Apollo using vertical technology to grow more with less space.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Even traditional vegetable farms like Kok Fah are using advanced greenhouses and irrigation systems to mitigate the impact of extreme weather changes on their crop growth.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Fish farms like Barramundi Asia are growing seabass in deep underwater netcages, just off Pulau Semakau.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Farms like Panasonic and Sustenir are growing vegetables in climate-controlled, multi-tiered indoor spaces.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Another company, ComCrop, is even growing vegetables on our rooftops!

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These are all innovative solutions that help us grow more food with less space, and we should explore more opportunities and options to scale these up.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To optimise limited space and increase production yields, we need to push technological boundaries.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We need to pursue water and energy efficiency.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We need to automate and we need to integrate the systems through robotics and sensors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We have to adapt our solutions to protect against climate change that affects the yields of the crops.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In response to Miss Cheng Li Hui's question on how we can help our coastal farms to mitigate consequences of coastal oil spills, this is one good example of how our farms can adopt technologies to protect themselves from untoward circumstances, especially those relating to environmental pollution or weather pattern changes.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Even some of our other farms, the bean sprouts farm, for example, and I have seen it for myself, are using technology to transform the way they pack their bean sprouts.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is a fairly automated process from how the bean sprouts are being put into a sorter, automatically weighed, put into packets, sealed and ready to get into the freezer and sent out to our shops.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Our egg farms as well have adopted a lot of automation such that the eggs are automatically collected on a conveyor belt, sorted by some form of infra-red scanning to make sure that the eggs are not broken, have no micro-cracks, and then sorted into size, and packed and ready to be shipped out as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Through technology, from my description, you will see that farming will begin to resemble an industrialised production process, much like any other factory we have.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It will also attract and excite a younger generation of tech-savvy Singaporeans to consider venturing into this industry seriously.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We need the right people to achieve our vision.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Our modern farmers should be more appropriately called "agri-technologists" or "agri-specialists", not just farmers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will need a generation of "agri-specialists" with multidisciplinary expertise.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Farming will no longer just be about horticulture, no longer just be about aquaculture.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It will no longer be just about toiling in the sun, doing manual labour, but about engineering, info-comm technology, entrepreneurship and R&D.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The interactions among these areas will generate ideas to transform the farming industry.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Apollo, as a vertical fish farm, has also adopted and invented some of their own technologies, their own software, their own sensors in the fish tanks, so much so that the operational room is an air-conditioned room where the operators sit in the room looking at computer monitors.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They can tell the water temperature, the salinity of the water.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They even have video cameras to tell how the fish are doing in the tanks and have automatic feeding as well to feed the fish in the tank.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In essence, this is a very high-tech process, and Apollo has worked with Temasek Polytechnic and Republic Polytechnic to provide internships for students in the agriculture course to be trained in using their high-tech systems.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Many young people in these Polytechnics are now excited to join Apollo in their venture, especially now that Apollo has gone overseas.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It means increasing demand for local produce, helping our farms to seek financing.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Consumers, Singaporeans, must also pay a part and actively support our local produce.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In other words, it is about creating an active ecosystem, an environment where our farms can thrive.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In this regard, the ICP pointed out that tight cash flows often limit the farmers from investing in more expensive technology.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The current APF co-funds investments in technology but only on a reimbursement basis after the farmers have spent their own money.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The account manager will facilitate the farmer's interactions with the many agencies and they will also work with stakeholders.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If they are willing and able to transform, AVA will walk this journey with them.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In fact, one of the things AVA has been actively doing is to help our farmers to understand technology better.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Just last year, AVA brought a group of our farmers to Japan to source for technology, to help them look at indoor farming technology which they may be keen to adopt.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This year, in April, we will be bringing a different group of farmers to other advanced farms in China to understand land-based farming and some of the technologies they can adopt in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This farm transformation map is just in its infancy.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will continue to work with ICP and other stakeholders to refine it as we gain momentum and as technology for farming matures.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Over the next few years, this partnership will create practical initiatives and solutions that I hope will be impactful for the farming industry.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Therefore, to respond to the Members, the Government has a strategy.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But it will not be without challenges going forward and we cannot do it alone.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We need the cooperation and support of our local agricultural practitioners to transform themselves and the entire sector.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I believe if we can do this well, we will have a "food story" to go along with our "water story".

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The agriculture sector is not the only sector that has to transform itself to prepare for the future.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The real estate sector also needs to change.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong asked how the Ministry will help our real estate industry overcome the challenges that are posed by digital disruption.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We are already seeing signs of such disruption in countries like the US, the UK and Australia where sophisticated online platforms have enabled consumers to conduct property transactions themselves.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They have used online property searches and viewing, as well as e-conveyancing and other value-added services.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We have also seen quite a number of do it yourself (DIY) property portals sprouting up in Singapore in recent years.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This has led to a growing number of Singaporeans choosing to complete their property transactions without the use of a property agent.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: To survive and thrive, the industry must consider new ways of doing things.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is one of the 23 ITMs being developed under the ITM.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Through the ITM, we hope to create a resilient and future-ready real estate industry that will continue to provide good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This will involve three broad thrusts: productivity, scale and skills.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: First, we must help our real estate companies maximise the potential of their workers and raise productivity.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This will allow them to remain competitive and continue to provide good jobs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On our part, Government agencies will consider how we can streamline processes to make the sector more productive, while providing consumers with added convenience and more positive experiences.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will also explore how to streamline other transactions, such as for rentals for private properties.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Our second thrust is to help companies scale up and take advantage of new growth areas.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: With scale, companies can leverage on greater economies of scale, increase their value proposition, and better respond to market disruptions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Several real estate companies have done this by expanding into related areas in the property value chain or by venturing overseas.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They have enhanced their value proposition by expanding downstream, from their original focus in space optimisation, to facilities management and shared services.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: LHN's efforts, with support from SPRING and International Enterprise (IE) Singapore, have allowed the company to take advantage of new areas of growth, including expanding into China, to manage mixed-use developments.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Expanding into new business areas or overseas markets is not easy.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is why, as part of the Real Estate ITM, we will work with the industry to identify new areas of growth and see how to support their efforts to deepen their expertise, develop competitive niches and enter overseas markets.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The third thrust is to ensure that our workers are equipped with the right skills.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As we work with the sector to raise productivity and pursue new areas of growth, there will be new ways of doing things and new jobs being created.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For example, with more information and services being online, it may be more important for property agents now to hone their skills in servicing clients and building up their credentials rather than just competing on marketing and closing transactions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will be working with companies, industry associations and unions to ensure that there are training opportunities to help workers upskill and continuously refresh those skills throughout their careers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Together, these thrusts will support a major transformation of the real estate industry.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But, as the CEO of Netflix, Reed Hastings, said, "Companies rarely die from moving too fast, and they frequently die from moving too slow." The time to transform is now.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Over the next few months, my colleagues from MND and the agencies will work closely with all stakeholders − companies, industry associations, workers and unions − to develop the ITM and the way they should take it forward.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong asked about using EUP to address the deterioration of public infrastructure in older private estates.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Public infrastructure in private estates is maintained by public agencies like NParks, LTA, and PUB.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If deterioration occurs and ad hoc repairs are needed, the public can alert the relevant agencies directly or through MSO's OneService app to do so.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong also asked about the master developer concept.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As this has been covered by Minister Lawrence Wong's speech earlier, I will not elaborate further.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong also asked about the option of thinking about using BID in our planning.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is something we will study and we will be able to release more details when the study is completed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Louis Ng made several suggestions to better tackle animal crime, including increasing the number of AVA inspectors for wildlife crime, introducing sniffer dogs to detect smuggled wildlife and working more closely with AWGs.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: AVA already works closely with AWGs on animal cruelty cases.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This has been found to be mutually beneficial and this cooperation has resulted in several successful investigations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I believe AVA is happy to engage more AWGs who can be helpful in this way.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked whether we can extend the funding and support for the Love Cats pilot project to more estates in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We are currently in the process of assessing the Cat Welfare Society's proposal, but we do need to recognise that there are differing views among residents on this subject.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We want to be a City in a Garden with its attendant flora and fauna.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For that to be a reality, all of us need to play a part in finding the right balance between human-animal interaction and conflict.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We expect pet owners to be responsible for their pets, just as we expect others to treat animals with respect and tolerance.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the possibility of labelling palm oil on food labels so that consumers can play their part in anti-haze efforts.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is an idea that requires further study.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For instance, requiring this labelling on food labels could help consumers make more conscious decisions no doubt.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: However, this would also be stricter than current international standards and may be misperceived as a trade barrier.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, for the moment, we have taken the approach of encouraging the industry to voluntarily declare that their palm oil is from sustainable sources.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources will talk more about the haze issue later in his COS session.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: While we move to tackle the challenges ahead, we must also support the vulnerable in our community.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Several Members asked whether we can do more for single parents.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There were suggestions to waive the resale levy, to allow flat applications before finalisation of divorce, to lift the debarment and raise the income ceiling for public rental, to have a dedicated appeals channel and to give more help to single unmarried parents.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Each may have their unique circumstances and challenges.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Let us think back to all the residents we see in our MPS.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There is no typical case of a single parent.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There is no classic case where you say it fits a certain profile.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They all have their unique social challenges, different family backgrounds and unique family situations.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We have addressed some of these challenges on how we help single parents in previous Parliamentary Questions.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But let me reassure Members once again that while certain rules and criteria are needed to achieve fair allocation and policy objectives, they are not applied in a blanket manner simply because there is no typical case, there is no typical profile.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Therefore, we take a case-by-case approach and apply flexibility, taking into account those factors I said earlier.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: A gentleman, let us just call him Mr A.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: He earns $1,800 monthly at a hawker stall.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: He is the sole breadwinner supporting his wife and two children and he sold his flat last year due to debts, a very common story that we may have encountered in our MPS.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They moved into a 2-room rental flat in Ang Mo Kio last month.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Another gentleman, let us call him Mr B.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: He earns $2,000 a month as a driver and he is close to retirement age.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: His wife is unable to work due to health issues and looks after their daughter.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They had been staying with a friend but now the friend asked them to move out, another common story.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Another case, Madam C, a lady in her 30s.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: She is a single mother, unmarried parent with three children who were born out of wedlock.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Her family turned her out and she could not turn to the children's biological fathers as they have moved out of Singapore − another sad but not unheard of type of story.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: She is unemployed as she needs to look after her children.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: HDB allocated them a 1-room rental flat in the northern part of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: All these families, and many others, were assisted by HDB because they were in need and had no other housing options and no family support, but each of them has a different story and different need at the same time.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin asked what is the best approach for single unwed parents to access housing.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I would say anybody who is in need is welcome to approach their MP for help, but they can also appeal to HDB directly.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The examples I gave earlier show that HDB does take a compassionate approach towards these cases in need.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: HDB will seek to understand the facts of each case and evaluate all appeals fairly and objectively, and apply help where necessary.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin also asked for an update on the ASSIST scheme.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin also asked about the underlying principle of why only applicants who sold the flat before a divorce can apply for the ASSIST scheme.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Therefore, those who were able to retain the matrimonial flat after divorce or those who are able to buy a flat after divorce − when they dispose of their old flat, they get some money and they are able to buy a flat on their own − will not qualify for the ASSIST scheme.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, their financial status is also something that we consider and whether they end up owning the matrimonial home subsequently.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That is why the scheme is designed this way.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Our housing policies address the majority of our population and there will always be a minority whose circumstances are not addressed.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The channels for appeal are always open to them.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And they are not intended to create extra friction.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Rather, it is to ensure fairness to the majority who have abided by the general policies.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I urge Members of this House and members of the public to approach the agencies for assistance when necessary.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Miss Cheryl Chan and Mr Pritam Singh asked whether HDB can offer rental flats to Singaporeans married to foreigners.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If they do not have Singaporean children, it is difficult to extend them the same level of subsidies as households with two or more Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Nonetheless, as the Member has acknowledged, HDB does exercise flexibility and HDB has made exceptions to help those families in extenuating circumstances, and we will continue to do so.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Separately, on the JSS in public rental, we agree with Mr Henry Kwek that flatmates provide company and support for each other.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For the minority who cannot get along, HDB advises them to seek mediation and, if that is unsuccessful, they may search for another eligible person or apply to rent another flat.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We do not intend to allow singles to stay alone, but we are working to address some of the issues through design.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: One of the emplaced families, the Lim family, visited the 2-room flexi flat show-flat at HDB Hub, and told us they were very excited at finally being able to have their own home.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Mrs Lim, in particular, cannot wait to do up her own kitchen.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is every woman's dream to want to have a nice kitchen, I suppose.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: My mother certainly would never compromise on the furnishings in the kitchen.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Many applicants have told us that the help offered by Fresh Start is useful, from the grant, to the concessionary rate loan and the capping of the resale levy.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Before Fresh Start, second-timer families would not have been eligible for any of these concessions, certainly not a second housing grant.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This shows that we do consciously review our housing policies to make them more inclusive and to help families who would otherwise not qualify again.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They are welcome to apply and HDB will take a case-by-case approach to assess their eligibility.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I am very excited for the emplaced families who have begun their journey back to home ownership.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is early days in this scheme and we look forward to welcoming more families to the scheme.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We have a little bit of time for clarifications.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: On the Temporary Loan scheme that the Minister announced earlier today, could he provide more details on who else will qualify for the scheme and how it will be rolled out?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: One, there has been a call for public participation in future development of these plans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: How will this be carried out and how can the public play a greater role?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: On the master developer scheme that was announced, these are huge projects.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: How will private Singapore firms be able to participate fully in these projects while competing with large-scale international firms and, of course, with public companies as well − and by "public", I mean Government companies.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: For the Senior Minister of State on prefabrication, the ICPH, I understand that the current Kaki Bukit plant run by SEF SpaceHub has a production of about 100,000 metres cube annually.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Does BCA have a target for the total number of ICPHs and also a production target by 2020?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: For the Minister of State Dr Koh Poh Koon, I know he did not touch —

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: I know he did not touch specifically on APF.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Could he share how many farms have applied for it so far and whether there are any hurdles that prevent more people coming forward?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The second question is on rejuvenation projects and urban projects.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We already do a lot of consultation for these projects.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We go to the community and we get feedback.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are doing this for the Rail Corridor, for example.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And for many of the projects which I talked about, in fact, all of them, be it the Kallang River Rejuvenation, Jurong Lake District, Punggol, we will have exhibitions, we will showcase the ideas and we will get feedback and inputs to improve on these ideas.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On local participation, this is already happening to the extent that these are Government projects and the Government is putting them out as a developer.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We do encourage local architects, consultants, engineers and contractors to take part.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In some instances, when it is a big master planning project, we will even require that foreign firms participating in the design of the master plan partner a local firm which has local knowledge of the environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will respond to the Member's question on ICPHs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I said earlier that there are four sites for ICPH already out.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, with these 10 ICPHs, a rough forecast would be that it should be able to provide up to 60% to 70% of the components we need locally and the rest from abroad.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A lot of it depends on how successful we are in persuading firms to take up DfMA.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Farmers gave feedback, especially ICP, that cash flow is often a problem when they want to scale in technology, which is why based on the feedback from farmers and from ICP, we have decided to restructure APF such that they can have 30% of the grants given upfront to allow them to scale in technology as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: My clarification is for the Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Has there been any case where the HDB levy payable by a flat applicant had been waived before?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We can do one or two things, that is, reduce the quantum or we can incorporate it into the loan so that it can be spread out over a longer period.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: I saw many beautiful pictures of other towns.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: My question is: will Yishun Swimming Complex be included in the $700 million projects?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: The second question: I have just clarified with the Singapore Contractors Association's President and he confirmed that contractors are seldom compensated in ECI.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: So, I would like to ask the Ministry whether there will be further studies to reduce wastage and compensate the contractors.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: He said, in the US, contractors are all compensated and only three contractors are called.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: The last question is on the Code of Practice, whether it would address the root cause, that is, not enough time is given to architects and engineers to do BIM modelling.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Otherwise, the Code of Practice will just add additional pressure on them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We encourage firms to follow these guidelines when they do ECI.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It aims to strike a right balance between certainty of getting the contracts and the amount of effort that you put in.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Certainly, we will encourage more firms to comply with these guidelines.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But for the public sector, this is what we do.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On the question about Yishun Swimming Complex, let me go back and check.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On the Code of Practice, as I said, it is being piloted.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are using this in some private sector projects to see whether architects, in compliance with the Code of Practice, will be able to put in the information necessary for contractors to use the BIM model in a way envisioned by BIM/VDC.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: After the pilot is completed, we will then know whether they work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When we launch them, the Member will be assured that the Code of Practice would have been tested.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: A quick clarification for Senior Minister of State Desmond Lee.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The tree inspection records − how long are they kept?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: I have a clarification for the Minister of State on private estate upgrading.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: I was not referring to ad hoc repair and maintenance work.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: And this will go a long way to resolving this issue.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: But these estates are already 50 years old, and they have to continue to wait out for more years.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, once we start with Batch Nine, we will then come up with a decent time for starting on Batch 10.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But if there are any estate areas that need urgent repairs because of wear and tear, then this is where I said that you can ask for ad hoc repairs at the moment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Second, similarly, will HDB specifically consider whether a single unwed parent can form a family nucleus with his or her child?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Third, for the short-term rental, I raised this during the debate on the Bill, when will we see the draft guidelines, when will it be available to the public for public consultation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Fourth, on the Love Cats programme, I understand that a review is going on, but this has already been done for two years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Is there a timeframe where we will finally make a decision?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Fifth, will AVA be considering the Wildlife Save a Dog programme?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Are they considering now and keeping it open?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Lastly, will we be increasing the number of wildlife inspectors?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I do not think the Minister has addressed that point.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: With regard to Interim Judgment for divorce cases − before the Final Judgment has been imposed, it will be hard to decide at that point in time who gets full care and control of the child.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Therefore, it is very hard at that point in time to allow application for a flat.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Also, sometimes the judge also determines who gets the matrimonial home, or the two parties may decide the way they want to split the assets.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Therefore, until the judgment is finalised and assets are well split, it is very hard to then allow the applicants to apply for a flat.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As for whether we want to consider a single unwed parent with a child as a family nucleus, as I said in my reply, HDB does take a very flexible approach to assess each case on a case-by-case basis and to apply flexibility.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For the Love Cats project, once the agencies, after engagement with stakeholders, have an interim review to engage the animal welfare groups further, we will release the outcome.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: For wildlife inspectors, today, in this day and age where technology is available, we should not just talk about more body counts, more people on the ground.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We should consider how we can leverage technologies to multiply the effects of people and perhaps also work closely with the animal welfare groups to be our eyes and ears on the ground as well to help in nabbing offenders.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I think we should take a broader approach rather than just look at employing more wildlife inspectors.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon, not more than two clarifications, please.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Could I have the response on property transactions undertaken by the Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs)?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Will he also look into the ABSD implications of such transactions?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, to the extent that ABSD, and buyer's stamp duty apply on the buy side, and seller's stamp duty apply on the sell side, then potentially they would also apply in the case when such shares are being transferred.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Alex Yam, would you like to withdraw the amendment without a lengthy preamble?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: My gratitude to Minister Lawrence Wong, Minister Grace Fu, Senior Minister of State Desmond Lee and Minister of State Koh Poh Koon for their enlightening answers and commitment to a future-ready city for all.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Therefore, it remains for me to beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
